overview.title: Convenience features and what Navide changes on your computer
overview.intro: Navide writes outside its own folder only when a convenience feature you allowed needs it. Every write is announced and logged; once you turn a feature off or delete its entry, Navide does not add it back.
overview.requiredHint: The panes it serves cannot run without it, so it has no switch. It is listed so you know about it.
overview.reasonRemoved: You removed what Navide wrote, so this is off. Use the switch to allow it again.
overview.noTargets: Navide has not written anywhere yet.
overview.confirmBody: Navide will remove what it wrote here (only entries Navide marked as its own):
overview.confirmBodyNone: Nothing Navide wrote is present, so nothing will be removed.

claude_hooks.name: Claude hooks: turn detection, Navide Guard and wake-up
claude_hooks.benefit: Claude reports when each turn ends, Navide Guard checks Claude's tool calls, and the push channel can wake an idle Claude.
claude_hooks.purpose: Navide knows when Claude finishes a turn and Navide Guard can check its tool calls
claude_hooks.writes: Only in the Claude panes Navide starts: they start with the hooks (turn detection, Navide Guard, wake-up); your ~/.claude/settings.json is not changed. Entries earlier versions wrote there are taken back at startup, with a backup; if they cannot be, the hooks in that file stay in use
claude_hooks.cost: Turn ends are guessed from output instead of reported; Navide Guard does not check Claude's tool calls; the push channel cannot wake an idle Claude.

qwen_hooks.name: Qwen hooks: turn detection and Navide Guard
qwen_hooks.benefit: Qwen reports when each turn ends and Navide Guard checks Qwen's tool calls.
qwen_hooks.purpose: Navide knows when Qwen finishes a turn and Navide Guard can check its tool calls
qwen_hooks.cost: Turn ends are guessed from output instead of reported; Navide Guard does not check Qwen's tool calls.

copilot_hooks.name: Copilot hooks: turn detection and Navide Guard
copilot_hooks.benefit: Copilot reports when each turn ends and Navide Guard checks Copilot's tool calls.
copilot_hooks.purpose: Navide knows when Copilot finishes a turn and Navide Guard can check its tool calls
copilot_hooks.writes: Only in the Copilot panes Navide starts: each pane's own hooks folder carries Navide's hook file; your ~/.copilot is not changed. The ~/.copilot/hooks/agent-team.json earlier versions wrote is taken back at startup, with a backup; if it cannot be, that file stays in use
copilot_hooks.cost: Turn ends are guessed from output instead of reported; Navide Guard does not check Copilot's tool calls.

codex_hook-trust.name: Codex hook trust carried over
codex_hook-trust.benefit: Codex panes keep the trust you already gave your own hooks instead of asking again.
codex_hook-trust.purpose: Codex panes do not ask you to trust your own hooks again
codex_hook-trust.writes: Only in the Codex panes Navide starts: the hooks you already trust are passed on the command line; your ~/.codex/config.toml is not changed. The [hooks.state] rows earlier versions wrote there are taken back at startup, with a backup; if they cannot be (or in a development build of Navide), rows are written there as before
codex_hook-trust.cost: Every Codex pane asks you to trust your own hooks again.

codex_login-promote.name: Share a Codex sign-in made in a pane
codex_login-promote.benefit: A Codex sign-in you make inside a pane becomes Codex's sign-in everywhere.
codex_login-promote.purpose: a sign-in made inside a pane works for Codex everywhere
codex_login-promote.writes: ~/.codex/auth.json (a hard link to the pane's sign-in)
codex_login-promote.cost: A sign-in made inside a pane stays in that pane.

grok_folder-trust.name: Grok folder trust shared
grok_folder-trust.benefit: A folder you trusted in one Grok pane is trusted in every Grok pane, including ones you open or rebuild later.
grok_folder-trust.purpose: Grok panes do not ask you to trust the same folder again
grok_folder-trust.writes: ~/.grok/trusted_folders.toml: when a Grok pane records that you trusted a folder, Navide appends that folder's entry to the end of this file. Only the workspace the pane was opened in, or a folder inside it, is shared to ~/.grok. Only folders the file does not already mention are added; your own entries, comments and layout are never changed. The file is backed up before every change, and turning this off removes exactly the text Navide appended, so the file is back to what it was (or removes the file if Navide created it)
grok_folder-trust.cost: A folder you trusted in one Grok pane is asked about again in every new or rebuilt Grok pane.

cursor_project-mcp.name: Navide MCP tools for Cursor
cursor_project-mcp.benefit: Cursor panes get Navide's MCP tools, such as messaging, plans and scheduling.
cursor_project-mcp.purpose: Cursor panes can use Navide's tools
cursor_project-mcp.writes: The workspace's .cursor/mcp.json and a line in .git/info/exclude
cursor_project-mcp.cost: Cursor panes have no Navide tools.

cursor_project-skills.name: Skills delivered to Cursor
cursor_project-skills.benefit: Skills you route to Cursor are linked into the workspace so Cursor panes can use them.
cursor_project-skills.purpose: Cursor panes can use the skills you routed to them
cursor_project-skills.writes: Links in the workspace's .cursor/skills/ and a line in .git/info/exclude
cursor_project-skills.cost: Cursor panes get no delivered skills.

credentials_auto-repair.name: Account sign-in auto-repair
credentials_auto-repair.benefit: When a CLI's live sign-in goes missing after an account switch, Navide restores the account you chose so panes do not start signed out.
credentials_auto-repair.purpose: panes do not start signed out after an account switch
credentials_auto-repair.writes: The CLI's live sign-in: Keychain, ~/.claude.json and the vendor's credential files
credentials_auto-repair.cost: A pane can start signed out after an account switch went wrong.

codex_pane-homes.name: Codex pane folders
codex_pane-homes.benefit: Each Codex pane gets a folder of its own so panes can use different accounts side by side.
codex_pane-homes.purpose: Codex panes can use different accounts side by side
codex_pane-homes.cost: Required: the panes it serves cannot run without it.

pane-shims.name: Pane launch folders
pane-shims.benefit: Kimi, Grok, Antigravity and Muse panes start from a folder of their own so each pane keeps its own account and settings.
pane-shims.purpose: each pane keeps its own account and settings
pane-shims.writes: ~/.navide-panes/, plus entries a pane creates moved into the vendor's own folder (~/.kimi-code, ~/.grok, ~/.gemini, ~/.agents, ~/.copilot, ~/.qwen) and empty seed entries created there; each move or creation is logged
pane-shims.cost: Required: the panes it serves cannot run without it.

claude_account-homes.name: Claude account folders
claude_account-homes.benefit: Each signed-in Claude account keeps a folder of its own, so sessions and settings follow the account.
claude_account-homes.purpose: sessions and settings follow each Claude account
claude_account-homes.writes: Links and moved files in ~/.claude for signed-in accounts
claude_account-homes.cost: Required: the panes it serves cannot run without it.

model.label: Model
model.shadowed-by-command: This CLI has a launch command set (Settings → CLI Agents). That line runs as written and Navide adds no model or effort to it, so neither can be picked here. Put the model in the launch command, or clear it.

refuse.model-unsupported: "{agent}" cannot be given a model at launch; opened this way it falls back to its default model. Remove the model and switch models inside the CLI instead.
refuse.effort-unsupported: "{agent}" has no separate effort setting. Remove the effort; if this CLI encodes the level in the model id (e.g. gpt-5.3-codex-high), put it in the model instead.
refuse.model-malformed: The model must be a single model id: no spaces, and it cannot start with "-". A value with spaces splits into two arguments, which hands the CLI an extra flag.
refuse.effort-malformed: The effort must be a single word: no spaces, and it cannot start with "-".

limits.hint: Optional limits that keep Navide and the agents it runs from overloading this machine. Each one is off, or at Navide's previous behavior, until you change it.
limits.test-workers: Cap test-runner workers in new panes
limits.test-workers-hint: New panes get NAVIDE_TEST_MAX_WORKERS. Repos that read it (this repo's vitest config does) run tests with at most that many workers, so several panes testing at once don't saturate the CPU. Panes already open keep their environment.
limits.evolve-reclaim: Reclaim self-evolution panes that time out
limits.evolve-reclaim-hint: When a self-evolution run passes its time limit without reporting, its pane is reclaimed (turned into a card you can resume with one click, never closed) once it is idle and this long has passed. Turn off to leave such panes running, as before.
limits.detached: Keep track of servers closed panes leave behind
limits.detached-hint: New panes get an inert NAVIDE_PANE_MARK variable. A dev server an agent started in the background inherits it, so after its pane is gone it can be listed here. Nothing is stopped unless you click Stop.
limits.detached-empty: No servers left behind by closed panes.
limits.focused-reclaim: Also reclaim the focused pane when it sits untouched
limits.focused-reclaim-hint: Idle reclaim (above) never takes the pane each window has in focus, so that pane keeps its CLI running however long it sits. With this on, a focused pane nobody has typed in or received output in for this long is reclaimed too — turned into a card you can resume with one click, never closed. A pane waiting for an answer or holding unsent text is still kept.
limits.spotlight-hint: Spotlight already skips node_modules and Navide's own hidden folders, but it indexes build output (dist, out, build) and extra worktrees in your repos, which can keep it busy while agents build and test. Navide does not change this for you: add those folders under Spotlight's search privacy list yourself.

nativeBackends.title: Native backends
nativeBackends.description: Some Navide plugins include native code. Navide runs it in a sandbox with no network access of its own; it can read only the workspaces you open with it, and change files only where you allow. A Navide plugin that also runs git, gh and glab commands (marked high risk below) can, through them, contact network hosts and send workspace data, and read and change workspace files without that permission. Nothing native runs until you turn the switch below on.
nativeBackends.enable: Allow third-party Navide plugins to run native backends

agentTools.enable: Let agents call tools from third-party Navide plugins
agentTools.description: Off by default. When on, agents in your panes can call the tools a third-party Navide plugin declares, once you have allowed that Navide plugin. A tool that changes files asks you once per workspace. With this off, Navide behaves as if no Navide plugin had tools.
agentTools.externalCallers: Let external MCP clients call them too
agentTools.externalCallersDisclosure: External programs share a single token, so the record of a call can only say "an external client", not which program it was. The Host credential is treated the same way.

Commands already started when you disable it or revoke its permission run to completion (up to about 30 seconds).

localInstall.replaceLocal: Replace the file version {version} of {id} with this file?
localInstall.replaceWithMarketplace: Replace the file version of {id} with Navide Marketplace version {version}?
localInstall.replaceResets: Replacing it clears the permissions, the native backend consent, the workspaces it may change files in and the agent tool approvals given to the installed version; you will be asked again, and Rollback cannot bring the replaced version back.
localInstall.replaceDataSetAside: The new version starts with an empty data folder. The existing data is kept aside, and the new version cannot read it.
localInstall.reattachData: Take back the data kept aside from this source earlier (off by default)
localInstall.takedownUnknown: Navide cannot tell right now whether this Navide plugin has been taken down: the Navide takedown list could not be fetched.

signatureState.verified: Signed by developer {publisher}, who passed Navide's developer vetting. This version itself was not reviewed by Navide.
signatureState.revoked: Signature no longer valid: Navide has revoked the signing key or the developer qualification of {publisher}.
signatureState.unverifiable: A signature Navide cannot check against a vetted developer ({publisher}): treat this file as unsigned.
signatureState.warningVerified: This Navide plugin comes from a file on this computer. It is signed by developer {publisher}, who passed Navide's developer vetting, but Navide has not reviewed this version. Only install files from people you trust.
signatureState.warningRevoked: This Navide plugin comes from a file on this computer, and its signature is no longer valid: Navide has revoked the signing key or the developer qualification of {publisher}. Navide has not reviewed it. Only install it if you trust where it came from.

errors.digestBlocked: This file of {id} cannot be installed: Navide has taken this exact file down (its digest is on Navide's blocked list).

trust.publisherRiskUnsigned: {publisher}'s package {id} is not signed by the Registry. Trusting this publisher lets Navide run its code.
trust.publisherRisk: Trust publisher {publisher} for {id}. A valid Registry signature proves package integrity, not that you want to run this publisher's code.
trust.backendRisk: {name} contains a native backend executable that can run with your user account's operating-system permissions.

capability.fs: Read and write files in your workspace.
capability.aiCli: Run the AI CLI agents set up in Navide.
capability.web: Can open and browse any website; site sign-ins are kept on this computer; agents use your sign-ins in this Navide plugin (they can send requests on websites for you) and can read every page it opens and its sign-in state; after you take over, agent scripts already running in a page stop only when you reload it; it can open many web pages at once, and each one uses memory.

extensions.inventoryRefreshFailed: Could not reload the installed Navide plugins: {error}
extensions.incompatibleReason: This version declares it needs Navide {version} or newer. It stays enabled, but may not work until you update Navide.

pack.countsLine: {total} Navide plugins · {ready} to install · {installed} already installed · {skipped} skipped
pack.membersNote: Each member is verified and confirmed on its own. Installing the pack never grants a permission you have not seen.
pack.summaryNote: Each Navide plugin below is verified and confirmed on its own. The pack itself asks for no permissions.
pack.partialNote: Skipped or cancelled members are not installed; members already installed stay (they can be uninstalled individually).
pack.restartNote: Newly installed Navide plugins are listed under Navide Plugins, where they can be started.

status.missing: Not in the Navide Marketplace, skipped
status.unavailable: Not available for this platform, skipped

pack.uninstallBody: This removes the pack. Its Navide plugins stay installed unless you tick them below.
pack.uninstallMembersHint: Installed only because of this pack:
pack.noPermissionsOfItsOwn: This pack grants no permissions itself; each Navide plugin in it asks for its own when you install it.

extensionsPolicy.fileScopesRepository: File scope (from the Git repository root)

voice.readback-model-missing: {voice} — Not installed. Reading with "{using}" for now.
voice.readback-model-missing-none: {voice} — Not installed, and this computer has no voice for the interface language.
voice.readback-model-other-os: Install better voices in your operating system's speech settings.
voice.readback-model-download-hint: In Accessibility › Spoken Content (just opened), click ⓘ / Manage Voices… next to System voice and download {voice}, then press Re-check.
voice.readback-hint: When a pane marked 🔊 finishes or needs your answer, a short notice is spoken with the system voice (for example "Navide is done"). Click 🔊 in a pane's title bar to mark it. Speech is synthesized on this computer; nothing is downloaded.
voice.readback-voice-hint: Auto picks the best system voice for the interface language, preferring Premium voices. Better voices can be downloaded in System Settings › Accessibility › Spoken Content.
voice.readback-voice-hint-windows: Auto picks the best system voice for the interface language. More voices can be added in Settings › Time & language › Speech.
voice.readback-voice-hint-other-os: Auto picks the best system voice for the interface language. Install more voices in your operating system's speech settings.
voice.readback-voice-none: No system voice matches the interface language; the system default voice will be used.
voice.readback-stop-hint: Press Esc or the voice input shortcut to stop reading at once.
voice.enabled-hint: Hold Ctrl+Alt+M (rebindable under Shortcuts) to dictate into the focused CLI pane. The text goes into its input box as if you typed it — nothing is sent until you press Enter yourself. Speech is transcribed on this computer by a local Whisper model; audio never leaves the machine.
voice.device-hint: Device names appear after the first voice use.
voice.device-missing-note: The chosen microphone is not connected; the system default will be used.
voice.shortcut-hint: The key to hold (or press) to dictate — a combination such as ⌃⌥M, a function key such as F13, one modifier by itself such as Right Option or Left ⌘ (a lone ⌘ or ⌃ starts once held by itself for a moment, so ⌘C and other shortcuts keep working), or fn (🌐) on a Mac. Changing it here also changes it under Shortcuts.
voice.shortcut-unbound: No shortcut — voice input cannot be started from the keyboard
voice.shortcut-meta-refused: {key} cannot be used in this recording mode: macOS does not report letting go of a key held with ⌘, so a held recording would never stop. Pick a chord without ⌘, such as ⌃⌥M, or set the recording mode to “Press to start, press again to stop”, where ⌘ chords work.
voice.shortcut-meta-warning: This shortcut uses ⌘, which only works in the “Press to start, press again to stop” recording mode: in this mode macOS does not report letting go of it, so a held recording will not stop. Reset it, rebind it, or switch the recording mode back.
voice.shortcut-typing-refused: {key} cannot be used: it types or edits in the CLI (and Enter / Esc already send / cancel), so holding it would type instead of dictate. Pick a function key such as F13, one modifier by itself such as Right Option, or a combination with ⌃ or ⌥.
voice.shortcut-taken-refused: {key} cannot be used: it is already the shortcut for {commands}. Pick another combination, or unbind it under Shortcuts first.
voice.shortcut-reserved-refused: {key} cannot be used: macOS uses it to {action}.
voice.shortcut-menu-refused: {key} cannot be used: the application menu takes it before Navide sees the key.
voice.fn-key-hint: The dictation shortcut is fn: hold it to dictate (a quick tap follows the recording mode); fn pressed together with another key (fn+arrow…) does not start a recording. Navide watches fn with a small helper that needs Input Monitoring permission.
voice.fn-status-no-permission: Navide needs Input Monitoring permission to see the fn key. Allow Navide under System Settings → Privacy & Security → Input Monitoring, then check again (if it still is not seen, quit and reopen Navide).
voice.fn-status-request-failed: Asking macOS for Input Monitoring permission failed (the fn helper did not answer). Allow Navide under System Settings → Privacy & Security → Input Monitoring yourself, then check again.
voice.fn-status-restarting: The fn key listener stopped; restarting…
voice.fn-status-failed: The fn key listener could not run.
voice.fn-status-missing: The fn key helper is missing from this copy of Navide, so fn cannot be seen. In a source checkout run pnpm build:fn-key (pnpm dev does it for you), then try again.
voice.fn-usage-conflict: macOS also acts on the 🌐 key ({action}). Set System Settings → Keyboard → “Press 🌐 key to” to “Do Nothing” so a press only dictates.
voice.mode-hold-tap-hint: Hold the shortcut to talk and let go to insert the text; a quick tap keeps listening hands-free until you press it again (up to 5 minutes).
voice.mode-hold-hint: Hold the shortcut while you speak; letting go inserts the text. Up to 60 seconds.
voice.mode-toggle: Press to start, press again to stop
voice.mode-toggle-hint: Press the shortcut once to start and again to insert the text; Esc cancels. Up to 5 minutes.
voice.script-hint: Whisper sometimes writes Chinese in Simplified characters; this converts every character to the chosen script. Words are not changed.
voice.status-unavailable: Status unavailable (the backend is not responding)
voice.sidecar-missing: Speech engine not found in this build
voice.engine-starting: Starting… (the first start can take up to a minute)
voice.engine-idle: Not running — it starts automatically when you press the shortcut
voice.engine-needs-model: Waiting for the speech model to be downloaded

general.auto-resume-reconnect: Resume sessions after a backend restart
general.resume-interrupted-on-launch: Resume working panes after restarting Navide
general.system-notify-hint: Show a desktop notification when a CLI finishes its turn or needs your input while Navide is in the background. The Dock badge keeps counting either way.
general.notify-sound-hint: Play a short chime on turn completion and a double ping when a CLI is waiting for you.
general.notify-permission-hint: macOS does not report the real authorization to Navide, so send a test notification and check it appears; if it does not, allow Navide under System Settings → Notifications.
general.auto-resume-reconnect-hint: When the backend crashes it takes every CLI process with it. Turn this on to resume the visible panes' conversations automatically once it comes back, instead of rebuilding each one by hand.
general.resume-interrupted-on-launch-hint: When Navide restarts, panes that were running a turn or waiting on a permission prompt or a question, plus the parent panes waiting on their reports, resume automatically (up to 6; the rest are marked "Working at restart"). Nothing continues on its own: press Continue, or let the parent tell it to. The parent is told which of its panes were interrupted.
general.confirm-close-pane-hint: Ask before the close-pane shortcut closes a CLI pane. A pane with a turn in progress always asks, regardless of this setting.
general.confirm-close-workspace-hint: Ask before the sidebar closes a workspace and its panes. That row ends every CLI pane in the workspace; their records are kept, so reopening it brings each one back as a card you click to resume. Plain “Close workspace” leaves the CLIs running and never asks.
general.idle-reclaim-hint: An idle CLI keeps holding the memory it allocated — often 200–300 MB each. Reclaiming ends the process and leaves the pane as a click-to-resume placeholder; the conversation is resumed from the CLI's own transcript. Never applies to the focused pane, a pane awaiting your answer, or one with unsent text.
general.idle-reclaim-after-hint: How long a pane must go without agent output or a keystroke before it is reclaimed.
general.idle-reclaim-now-hint: End those CLIs now instead of waiting for the threshold. {count} pane(s) qualify, holding roughly {size}. Each one becomes a click-to-resume placeholder.
general.idle-reclaim-now-empty: No pane qualifies right now — the focused pane, one awaiting your answer, one with unsent text and one that cannot be resumed are never reclaimed.
general.default-editor-hint: Where Navide opens files and folders. Diff views always use the Mini-IDE.
general.default-editor-custom-command-hint: Placeholders: {'{'}file{'}'}, {'{'}dir{'}'}, {'{'}line{'}'}, {'{'}workspace{'}'}. Run directly, not through a shell.
general.default-editor-custom-command-empty: Enter a command — until then Navide keeps opening files in the Mini-IDE.

appearance.theme-hint: Theme is a user-level preference applied across all workspaces.
appearance.reset-colors-hint: Reset all custom colors to the built-in theme
appearance.language-hint: Language is a user-level preference applied across all workspaces.
appearance.ui-scale-hint: Scale the whole interface — text, icons, and spacing — in every window. Separate from the terminal and editor font sizes, which keep their own ⌘= / ⌘- shortcuts.
appearance.restore-windows-hint: Reopen the workspace windows you had open when you last quit.
appearance.tweaks-hint: Tweaks are layered on top of the current theme and preserved when switching themes.
appearance.environment-hint: Re-run the first-launch environment detection wizard (checks Homebrew / Node / CLI / Ollama, etc.).
appearance.backend-timeout-hint: How long to wait for the backend to become healthy on startup or restart before giving up. Raise this on slower machines (15–120 seconds).
appearance.resume-behavior-hint: What happens to a workspace's previously spawned CLI panes when you open it.
appearance.restore-scope-hint: When always resuming, choose one CLI, the current Grid page, the active tab, all CLIs, or Auto — only the CLIs that were running when Navide last closed (all CLIs and Auto start two at a time, in order).
appearance.resume-concurrency-hint: How many CLI panes may resume at the same time when opening a workspace or restoring a layout; the rest queue. Lower this if resuming many panes at once causes 'terminal.create timeout' errors (1–10).

roles.title: Roles
roles.reset-confirm-body: All custom roles will be removed. This action cannot be undone.

nav.caption: The left half of the Settings window: the search box, and the grouped list of pages. Drawn in HTML, so it follows whichever theme you use.

search.label: Search box
search.text: Matches titles, sections and keywords across every page, up to eight hits; the grey text on the right of a hit is the group it belongs to.

groups.label: Groups
groups.text: Pages are listed in groups, and a group heading is not itself clickable. The list here is drawn in the order the real sidebar uses.

active.label: The open page
active.text: The selected row is filled in. Clicking a search hit switches to its page and scrolls to the section it names.

resource.caption: The Resource Manager window. Figures and scans update only when you press Refresh.

totals.label: The three cards on top
totals.text: CPU, memory and disk. The disk card stays blank until you press Scan — opening the window does not scan on its own.

rows.label: One row per pane
rows.text: Under the name is its workspace and vendor; the trend is a sparkline of the last few samples, and the two columns on the right are CPU and memory. The dot colour is the pane's state.

actions.label: Two actions per row
actions.text: Clicking the name jumps to that pane; Reclaim downgrades it to a placeholder. There is no force quit.

settingsSystem.intro: What each of the nineteen settings tabs controls, how Navide Cloud links several machines into one private network, and the system surfaces that live outside the main screen — the menus, the standalone windows, the usage views and resource upkeep.

s1.title: Settings overview
s1.p1: The settings window opens with ⌘,; the gear button in the title bar is the same entry point. The left sidebar is split into five groups, 24 tabs in total.
s1.p2: Below the sidebar heading is a search field with the placeholder Search settings…. It matches setting titles, their section and their keywords across tabs (using the current interface language and indexed keywords), listing at most 8 results; clicking one switches to that tab and scrolls to the section (with one exception: "Storage" closes settings and opens the Resource Manager directly). With no match it shows No matching settings. Esc clears it.

callout.title: The search index is not exhaustive
callout.text: The index is a hand-maintained list, and the {layout}, {notifications}, {security} and {channels} tabs have no entries at all, so nothing inside them is searchable — you have to open them yourself. A CLI Agents entry opens one CLI's settings drawer directly (see the "CLI Agents & Accounts" topic).

general.what: Close confirmation, idle reclaim threshold, resume behavior, default editor, quota badge, environment check, backend timeout, plus exporting and importing the whole settings bundle

appearance.what: Theme and custom colors, interface scale, restore windows

language.what: Interface language for every workspace: Traditional Chinese, English, or Japanese

statusBadges.what: The names and colors of the nine pane states

layout.what: The five-slot shell, which slot each view lands in, layout presets

notifications.what: Desktop notifications and the completion chime for CLI turns, plus the macOS permission check

voice.what: Hold-to-talk voice input transcribed on this machine: shortcut, microphone, recording mode, Chinese output, model and engine
voice.more: The "Voice input" chapter of the "{workspace}" topic

cloud.what: Cross-device link status, this machine's fingerprint, who may command this machine

credentials.what: A read-only scan of the credential and key risks on this machine: findings, inventory, scan roots and reminders
credentials.more: the page itself; it only scans and never changes a file

cliAgents.what: Installation, launch arguments and permission mode for each CLI

cliExtensions.what: Each AI CLI's own CLI extensions and hooks (a read-only inventory)

analyzer.what: The local inference backend, model downloads, model benchmarks

security.what: Navide Guard's rules and levels, protected branches, custom rules, and command protection for plain terminals

channels.what: Connect chat-app bots such as Telegram or Slack to CLI panes: bots, pairing, allowlist, account linking

mcp.what: Adding, enabling and inspecting MCP servers

skills.what: The shared skill library and the routing matrix

prompts.what: The prompt skill library (the whole prompt the ∞ button casts)

memory.what: The instruction files of each CLI (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md and friends)

extensions.what: The execution policy Navide plugins run under, plus the bundled and installed Navide plugins; at the bottom, the disclosure overview of every Navide plugin installed from the Navide Marketplace (records only, it changes nothing a Navide plugin may do)

marketplace.what: Searching the Navide plugin registry and installing from it

updates.what: The three-stage check / download / install toggles

help.what: Read-only reference: the topic tabs along the top switch between the manual pages
help.more: the tab you are reading right now

s1.note: The Help tab holds no settings at all: it is a row of topic tabs, one page per topic, and the one you are reading is "Settings & System". Individual settings tabs do not carry help of their own — all of it lives here. When settings search matches a help entry it switches to the Help tab and jumps to the matching topic; in the other direction, neither the main window nor the native menus has an entry point straight to it, so settings is the only way in. Moving the whole set of settings to another machine lives in General ▸ Settings management (section 2), not at the bottom of the window.

s2.title: General, Appearance, Language, Status badges

confirmClose.desc: Ask before ⌘W closes a pane. A pane in the middle of a turn always asks, regardless of this toggle.

confirmCloseWorkspace.desc: Ask before the sidebar closes a workspace. Closing ends every CLI pane in it and removes their records — reopening will not bring them back.

reclaimIdle.desc: The master switch for idle reclaim (see section 3 of the "Workspaces & panes" topic).

reclaimAfter.desc: 15 minutes / 30 minutes / 1 hour / 3 hours / 8 hours / Never.

reclaimNow.desc: Reclaim right now without waiting for the threshold; next to it is how many panes qualify and roughly how much memory they hold.

resumeOnOpen.desc: What happens to old panes when a workspace opens: Always resume / Always start fresh / Ask each time.

resumeScope.desc: How far resume reaches: One CLI / Current Grid page / Active tab / All CLIs / Auto (only the CLIs running when Navide last closed).

resumeAfterRestart.desc: A backend crash takes every CLI process with it; with this on, the panes on screen resume automatically once it is back.

resumeInterrupted.desc: After you restart Navide, panes that were working (and the parents waiting on them) resume automatically, up to 6, without continuing on their own; the parent is told which ones were interrupted.

concurrentResume.desc: How many panes resume at once (1–10); the rest queue. Lower it if you see terminal.create timeout.

defaultEditor.desc: Mini-IDE / the system default application / a detected editor / a custom command, with Re-detect to scan again. A custom command can use {'{'}file{'}'}, {'{'}dir{'}'}, {'{'}line{'}'} and {'{'}workspace{'}'}, and is executed directly rather than through a shell. Changing it does not change diffs — diff views always use the Mini-IDE.

quotaBadge.desc: Show the remaining quota in the pane title, with a refresh interval (1 / 5 / 15 / 30 minutes).

environment.desc: ↻ Re-run environment check runs the first-launch environment detection wizard again (Homebrew, Node, the CLIs, Ollama and so on).

backendTimeout.desc: How many seconds to wait for the backend, 15–120; raise it on a slow machine.

settingsBundle.desc: Two buttons, Export Settings Bundle and Import Settings Bundle, with a scope badge and the config file path beside them. The bundle carries Roles, Pipelines, MCP, Analyzer and appearance preferences; API keys and tokens are redacted, and an import never overwrites a value you already have. It is a plain local file exchange — no share code, no sign-in, no connection needed.

appearance.theme: Theme — five built in: Dark (GitHub), Midnight, Forest, Light and High Contrast, with Dark (GitHub) as the default.
appearance.colors: Custom Colors — eight overridable color tokens (background, surface, text, secondary text, border, accent, success, danger). Overrides sit on top of the current theme and are kept when you switch themes; ↺ Reset to defaults restores them.
appearance.uiScale: Interface Scale — the first row of the Appearance ▸ Other block, and a dropdown rather than a slider: six steps (80%, 90%, 100%, 110%, 125%, 150%; 100% by default), on ⇧⌘= / ⇧⌘- / ⇧⌘0. It drives Electron's page zoom rather than a CSS variable, so text, icons, borders and spacing all move together, and the main process applies it to every window, Navide plugin windows included. It is a separate axis from pane font size: ⌘= / ⌘- / ⌘0 change only the terminal content font size (one value shared by every CLI pane in the window), while Interface Scale changes the shell around it — and the two multiply, the way a browser's page zoom multiplies with a site's own font size.
appearance.restore: Restore Windows — reopen the workspace windows that were open when you last quit.

callout.title: Notifications and sound live on the Notifications tab
callout.text: The notification toggles do exist — they are simply not on Appearance but on the Notifications tab, three of them: System notifications (a desktop notification when a CLI finishes its turn or needs your input while Navide is in the background; the Dock badge keeps counting either way), Notification sound (a short chime on turn completion and a double ping while a CLI waits for you), and Notification permission — macOS does not report the real authorization to Navide, so this one can only send a test notification for you to confirm it appears; if it does not, allow Navide under System Settings → Notifications. That last row only appears on platforms where it applies.

s2.language: Language is a tab of its own, not part of Appearance. Three languages: 繁體中文, English, and 日本語. Until you pick one, Navide follows the system language (Traditional Chinese when the system language is none of the three). This is a user-level preference and applies to every workspace.
s2.p1: Rename and recolor each of the nine pane states. The Chinese, English, and Japanese names are filled in separately (24 characters each; leave one blank to fall back to the built-in translation). Once changed, the pane badges, the sidebar, the meeting bar and the resource panel all follow. The setting lives on your account, not with the project.

statusTable.when: When a pane is in it

idle.when: A turn is finished and it is waiting for you at the prompt

awaiting.when: Stuck on a permission confirmation or a question

error.when: It failed to launch, or the terminal errored

waiting.when: A restored placeholder card that was never opened (list only)

disconnected.when: The backend session was lost (list only)

s2.note: Ten colors (Green / Yellow / Orange / Red / Blue / Purple / Pink / Cyan / Grey / Ink), all of them theme tokens, so they stay legible under any theme. Reset per row, Reset all for the page.

s3.title: Skills, Prompts, Memory
s3.p1: A skill is a folder containing a SKILL.md that says "when you meet this kind of task, do it like this". This page (titled Managed Skills) does three things: show every skill each CLI holds, decide who receives which one, and create new skills.

callout1.title: The shared root
callout1.text: Skills created by Navide always live in ~/.agents/skills. This page never moves or rewrites the skills inside a CLI's own folder — those are merely reflected so you can see them, and can be routed to other CLIs. (The one explicit exception is Move into shared library, which moves the files and leaves a symlink behind, and can be undone.)

s3.p2: The page has two views, Browse (cards) and Route (the routing matrix). The matrix has the 15 CLIs across the top and the skills down the side, each cell in one of four states, and every row carries All / None batch buttons:

on.meaning: A new pane will (or will not) be given this skill; each cell toggles individually.
on.who: 11: antigravity, claude, codex, copilot, cursor, grok, kimi, muse, opencode, pi, qwen

native.meaning: It reads ~/.agents/skills by itself, without Navide routing, so it cannot be turned off individually either (the cell is not clickable).
native.who: 6: codex, copilot, cursor, grok, muse, opencode

none.meaning: That CLI has no notion of skills at all, so there is nothing to connect to.

pending.meaning: It has a skills mechanism but Navide has not wired it up yet.

s3.p3: Clicking a skill opens a drawer. Skills Navide created itself are fully editable: Description, User invocable (lets you call it directly), Model invocation (lets the model pick it), Instructions (Markdown), and Advanced agent fields (allowed/disallowed tools, model, effort, context). Attachments are read-only; press Open folder to manage them. Known fields are editable and any other frontmatter is preserved verbatim; deletion is Move to Trash. If a CLI has a skill of its own under the same name, it is labelled Native skill wins — its own copy takes precedence.
s3.liveRefresh: The page refreshes itself: when an agent adds, installs or re-routes a skill over MCP, the list and the cards follow immediately — no need to close and reopen it. An unsaved draft of yours is never overwritten; a genuine collision raises the conflict prompt and you choose which version to keep.
s3.p4: This is a different thing from Skills above. A prompt skill is a whole reusable instruction, cast by the ∞ button in the pane title bar. One skill is one complete prompt — picking a skill "replaces" the prompt rather than appending to another one.

prompts.cast: Pressing ∞ directly casts the default skill (the one marked ★ Default in the list).
prompts.ring: Hovering over ∞ for about 0.3 seconds fans the other skills out into a ring below the button to pick from; moving the cursor toward the ring gets a short grace period, so it does not collapse immediately.
prompts.overflow: With more than 5 available skills, or in a pane narrower than 320px, it becomes a vertical list with exactly the same skills and keys.
prompts.preview: Pointing at any of them shows a preview card: the icon, the name, the full prompt text, and the turn cap.
prompts.keyboard: Keyboard: on ∞ press ↓ to open it, arrow keys to move, 1–9 to cast directly, Esc to close.
prompts.disabled: Disabled skills stay on the settings page but disappear from the ring.

s3.note: Each skill takes a Name, Icon, Summary, Prompt sent on cast, Resume text (blank uses the global resume text), Turn cap (0 = unlimited) and Category; each entry offers Set as default, Enable / Disable, Duplicate and Delete.
s3.h3: Memory — the instruction files of each CLI
s3.p5: Every CLI reads an instruction file before it starts work — CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, QWEN.md, .cursor rules. This page lists files, not CLIs: one row per file, with every CLI that reads it listed behind it, and the file is editable in place.

memory.levels: Split into User level (the home directory) and Project level (the current workspace). With no folder open, only the user level is listed.
memory.notCreated: A file that does not exist yet is marked Not created — saving creates it, along with any missing parent directories.
memory.reload: If another program changes the file while you are editing, it stops and asks you to Reload from disk (discards your draft) first, rather than overwriting your work or theirs.

s3.p6: The CLI coverage block at the bottom sorts the 15 CLIs into three groups:

mapped.value: Navide knows where this CLI keeps its instructions. 14 of them are in this group.

configured.value: Only aider. It has no file name of its own — it reads whatever the read: field in .aider.conf.yml names, so whatever you put there is what is listed here (up to 20). CONVENTIONS.md is only a name suggested by the documentation; the program itself does not know it.

unmapped.value: CLIs whose path Navide does not know. Currently empty.

callout2.title: cursor's user level is conditional
callout2.text: cursor has no dedicated user-scope loader; it walks up from the current folder to the filesystem root. So the rules in your home directory are only read when the project happens to sit below the home directory; a project on an external disk will not see them. This page still lists them, but cursor is the only CLI with no "standard file" at all, so Navide never offers to create one for it. Note also that copilot has a project level only, with no user-level instruction file.

s4.title: Shortcuts, Updates, Analyzer, Navide Plugins
s4.p1: The table has four columns: Command, Shortcut, Active when (the context it applies in) and Source.

shortcuts.record: Clicking a key box starts recording in place; + adds a second binding; ✕ removes one. A chord is at most two steps.
shortcuts.instant: Changes are written to keybindings.json immediately and applied to every open window; there is no save button.
shortcuts.search: The search field matches command names and key notation at the same time (both cmd+shift+p and ⌘⇧P find it); three filters, All / Customized / Conflicts.
shortcuts.conflicts: Conflicts marks bindings that collide and explains whether one always wins or they are kept apart by Active when.
shortcuts.reset: Reset to default per row, Reset all for the page. Export / Import move the settings, and import replaces rather than merges: it first tells you how many entries were discarded and how many imported, and lists the rejected ones.

callout.title: Two keys you cannot unbind, and a class of keys where unbinding does nothing
callout.text: "Open settings" and "open keyboard shortcuts" are the only way back into settings, so their last binding carries a 🔒 rather than an ✕ — you may rebind them, but not remove them. Separately, keys claimed by the application menu are marked ⚠: the menu takes those before the app ever sees them, so unbinding them here does not stop them.

s4.note: A binding removed with ✕ is recorded in keybindings.json as a -command rule (the command name with a leading minus). That is the notation to use when editing the file by hand. At the very bottom of the page are two further read-only reference tables, for the terminal and for the application menu.
s4.p2: Updating is split into three stages, each with its own toggle, so you can compose behavior such as "check automatically but do not download automatically":

checkFailures.toggle: Tell me when update checks keep failing + how many consecutive failures before it tells you (1–10)

s4.p3: Install updates when you quit defaults to off on purpose: installing always restarts the app, so leaving it off means "I decide every time". The page shows the current version, Check for updates, and a three-stage Check → Download → Install progress track. The update channel dropdown currently offers Stable only, with Beta marked "not available yet".
s4.p4: The update badge in the status bar covers these states: v{'{'}version{'}'} ready, a download percentage, Update failed and Update check failed. The announcement center also offers Download and Restart to install directly (see section 6 of the "Workspaces & panes" topic).
s4.p5: What you configure here is a small local model that Navide uses to read intent for pipelines; it has nothing to do with the CLI agents you use in panes. Three parts:

analyzer.backend: Inference backend — first pick one of two backends, Ollama REST or llama.cpp. llama.cpp needs the llama-cli path (with an auto-detect button and a file browser) and an optional GGUF model path; Ollama needs the inference URL (http://localhost:11434 by default). Both have a health indicator next to them.
analyzer.models: Model manager (Ollama mode) — type a model name and press ⬇ Download, with a progress bar; below it the installed models are listed (name, parameter count, size) and can be deleted one by one.
analyzer.benchmark: Model benchmark — runs four tasks against every local model: tech-stack detection (JSON output), a one-sentence workspace summary, picking the most relevant entry from a document list, and parsing CLI output into a question and its options. The results table ticks each item off with its duration, and at least three of the four (≥75%) must pass; models that do not pass are hidden from the model dropdown.

s4.p6: Below the policy block sits the Navide plugin inventory, in two parts: Bundled (packages shipped with the app, such as Bundled Git, which can be disabled and then Restored) and Installed (ones you installed yourself, listing their sensitive capabilities and dependencies, with Remove). Every row in both parts carries an extra line with its Manifest Permissions and Package-version Grant, spelling out what this version was actually granted; with no matching grant it says so. Searching the registry and installing new packages is now its own tab, Navide Marketplace — not here.
s4.p7: Installing takes up to two confirmations, each shown only when needed, and nothing is written to disk before them: if the publisher is not trusted yet, "trust the publisher" comes first — the screen says plainly that a valid signature only proves the package was not tampered with, not that you are willing to run this publisher's code; if the package carries a risk that needs confirming, "confirm the Navide plugin's permissions" follows, listing the sensitive capabilities it asks for and warning specifically when it ships a native backend executable. When neither applies, it installs straight away.
s4.extRollback: When the host has a package to go back to, the row gains "{toBundled}" or "{toVersion}": after a confirmation it rolls back to the package it displaced, and "{restart}" finishes the switch. A refused or failed rollback shows the host's own reason, translated, and a failed one restores the views it took down.
s4.extPrerelease: Each Navide plugin's row has a "{prerelease}" box, so pre-releases are opted into per Navide plugin; the Navide Marketplace's version list marks which versions are pre-releases and can install one directly.
s4.extNative: {native}: a third-party Navide plugin may ship its own backend program, which never runs by default. Turn on "{nativeEnable}", then press "{allow}" for that exact version of the Navide plugin. It runs in a sandbox with no network of its own (Seatbelt on macOS, bubblewrap on Linux), can read only the workspace opened with it and write only where you allow; a Navide plugin that also runs git, gh and glab commands (shown as high risk) can, through them, contact network hosts, send workspace data and change workspace files, and commands it already started finish even after you disable it; any change to the program or its permissions asks again. Windows is not supported yet.
s4.marketplace: The "{marketplace}" tab: search, filter by category, sort by downloads, last update or rating, hide incompatible entries, with up to three "{featured}" at the top. A detail page has the README, changelog and version list, with permissions and compatibility beside them; ratings are read-only here — rating or reporting a Navide plugin happens on the registry website after signing in. An entry badged "{pack}" installs a whole set with "{packInstall}"; removing a pack never removes a member another installed pack still uses. A navide:// link only opens the Navide plugin's detail page; pressing Install is always left to you.
s4.mirror: The download mirror: every release's files are published twice, on the GitHub Release and on dl.navide.dev — the same bytes, with sha256 sums to check them against. The mirror is the default update source: the app points its feed at dl.navide.dev on startup, and GitHub is the fallback. It falls back only on a network-shaped failure (unreachable host, timeout, 5xx/429), and once it has, it stays on GitHub for the rest of the session — only a restart goes back to the mirror. A 404 or a signature/checksum error never triggers the fallback — both hosts carry the same files, so it would fail the same way, and reporting the failure as it is helps more than hiding it.
s4.policyIntro: The execution policy decides what a Navide plugin's backend may execute. It is not a tab of its own: it is the block at the top of the Navide Plugins page, with its own scope badge (per user and per workspace) and policy file path. The top of it shows the effective policy — its source, its mode, and its status: active, stale, unavailable or corrupt.

policy.hostDefault: Host default — the built-in least-privilege baseline, marked read-only. It stays usable even if the user policy store is gone entirely, so there is always a way back.
policy.user: User policy — the global one, used wherever a workspace selects the User source; it reads "not created" until you make it. Three modes: full, allowlist, denylist. You can set the system namespaces and the shell executables, and the latter takes top-level executable names only — no paths, no shell expressions.
policy.highRisk: Full and denylist both need an explicit checkbox before they save, and the screen says why: full mode allows arbitrary executables (high-risk tools included) and system capabilities, while denylist mode is allow-by-default — listing names does not narrow what it actually grants, which is why Navide treats it as a high-risk choice too.
policy.source: Workspace policy source — each workspace picks Host default, User policy or Repository policy. A repository recommendation is labelled "untrusted" until you have read it and pressed "Accept repository policy", and switching sources requires an exact fingerprint match; if it changes after you reviewed it, it becomes "changed since review" and has to be re-checked. With no workspace open, this block cannot be used.
policy.recovery: Global policy store — its state is healthy, missing, corrupt, unsafe entry, or an unsafe/unavailable directory. A corrupt store can be rebuilt behind a confirmation checkbox; a rebuild replaces only the global policy and revision files and keeps every workspace source selection and repository policy file. When the store is judged unsafe, automatic rebuilding is disabled and the screen asks you to fix the host-owned paths it lists yourself.
policy.failClosed: Every unhealthy state is fail-closed: nothing is permitted until you pick a usable source or repair the broken one. That includes an uncertain save — the message reads "the result of the policy change could not be confirmed; the policy stays fail-closed, please re-check".

s4.policyNote: To clear every repository source pin at once, use "Reset all policy source selections", also behind a confirmation checkbox. It does not modify or delete any repository policy file; it only makes each workspace resolve against the global host default or user policy again.
s4.extNote: Where a misbehaving Navide plugin backend stops: only an overflow of protocol frames (request / response / cancel) is fatal to that backend. An overflow of host notifications is dropped and counted instead, so one noisy backend no longer takes the whole Navide plugin down, and a backend that exits cleanly records why rather than vanishing silently.

s5.title: Navide Cloud
s5.p1: Navide Cloud links your machines into a private network so that an agent on this one can send a message to an agent on another. The two entry points have clearly separate jobs:

entries.account: The account window — the cloud icon to the left of the gear in the title bar, or the menu Window ▸ Navide Cloud. Signing in, pasting a token, signing out, pairing and trust management all live here.
entries.settings: Settings ▸ Navide Cloud — link status, this machine's fingerprint, and the authorization rules. Everything to do with signing in is read-only on this page, and the page itself points you at that title-bar button.

s5.p2: While signed out, the account window has three tabs: Sign in, Create account and Use a token.
s5.p3: It uses email and a password (at least 8 characters); there is no magic-link sign-in, and the display name may be left blank. Registering sends a verification email, with Check now and Resend in the window; verification is soft — being unverified does not block you, and is only required when you want to invite someone else. Use a token is the advanced route: paste an access token issued by the server, and once it is in the system keychain it is never shown again.

callout1.title: There is no password reset yet
callout1.text: The account creation page says so itself: there is no password reset flow yet, so keep yours safe.

s5.p4: The server address is hard-coded; there is no field for it in settings, and the account window only shows it as a read-only Server row. There are six link states: Not signed in, Connecting…, Waiting for Keychain, Connected, Cannot reach the server and Access token rejected. The Your network block has a Turn off / Turn on switch to go offline temporarily, keeping the account and the settings.
s5.p5: Once both machines are signed in to the same account, the other appears in the Your network list (with Online/Offline, when it was last seen, and how many panes it has open).
s5.roster: The list is three levels deep: by device first (each heading folds; anything that is not this machine starts folded), then by state into Running, Idle and Not opened (an empty state is skipped entirely, and Not opened starts folded), and inside each state the workspace name is a caption rule between runs of panes. Three count tiles sit on top: click one to see only that state. The search box beside them matches pane name, workspace, CLI type and device name, and while you search the grouping is dropped in favour of a flat list of hits. Each row shows how long ago the pane started, with the exact timestamp on hover. Fold state is remembered on this machine.

pairing.step2: The same six digits appear on both screens, along with the other device's fingerprint.
pairing.step3: The screen reads "Check that {'{'}device{'}'} is showing these same six digits." — you have to compare the digits on the two screens with your own eyes.
pairing.step4: The initiating side presses They match / They do not match; the receiving side presses Allow pairing / They do not match. Either side can press Later to set it aside.
pairing.step5: Pairing only really happens once both sides confirm. A one-sided confirmation only shows "You confirmed. Waiting for the other device."

callout2.title: Different digits mean something is in between
callout2.text: The interface puts it like this: "Different digits on the two screens means something is in between. Refuse, and nothing pairs." This step is the foundation of the whole trust model — do not press match just because comparing is a nuisance.

s5.note1: A pairing code expires (after about five minutes) and exists only in memory — restarting the backend forgets a pairing in progress, and you simply start again. The receiving side does not have to open anything; the request appears by itself in the top right corner. The Pair button only appears for a device that is online, not yet paired, and under your own account; someone else's device has to knock first.
s5.p6: Every device is in one of three states: Paired, Not paired or Blocked; your own is always labelled This device. The Needs you block at the top of the account window collects two kinds of item:

pairing.content: A device knocked but has not been approved.

accessRequest.content: "{'{'}device{'}'} wants to reach {'{'}pane{'}'} in {'{'}workspace{'}'}", with the number of attempts.

s5.p7: Approve grants a very narrow scope — the interface says plainly: "Approving writes a rule for exactly this pane. Nothing else on this device is granted." Later only tucks it out of the list; it comes back the next time they try.

trust.block: Blocking: the Blocked block lists blocked devices, and Unblock lifts it. A block comes before every rule, and stops even your own other devices.
trust.unpair: Unpairing: Unpair on a device row, described as "Forget this device. It is not blocked." — it forgets the device without blocking it; the next time it appears it is treated as a first meeting, and the other side is notified too. It works while the other device is offline as well.

s5.p8: The Device identity block posts notices about identity anomalies, and the one to watch is a changed key: its messages are refused outright, the screen lists both "the fingerprint we remember" and "the fingerprint that arrived", and it deliberately offers no buttons at all — the interface wants you to check with that machine's owner in person first. Separately, if a device that has always sent encrypted messages suddenly sends one in the clear, that one is blocked too and logged.
s5.p9: The rules card in Settings ▸ Navide Cloud is titled Who may command panes on this device. It governs messages arriving from other devices only; agents on this machine are unaffected.

rules.denyAll: Deny by default: "Nothing is allowed by default: a message is refused unless a rule below matches it."
rules.shape: A rule is "From (which account, which device) → May reach (which workspace, which pane)", and a blank field means no restriction.
rules.ownDevices: There is a ready-made toggle, Allow my own other devices: any device signed in to the same account may reach any pane here, including ones added later.
rules.online: The rules live on the server and can only be changed while connected; offline, what you see is the last copy received.
rules.signed: The rules are signed with this device's key. If "Your rules could not be verified" appears, nothing is accepted until they are verified — press Sign rules now to re-sign them.

s5.p10: An address has three parts, <device>/<workspace>/<pane>. Two parts, <workspace>/<pane>, means the same machine, and one part is a pane name in your own workspace. Local resolution always wins; only when nothing local matches is the cross-device roster consulted. The device part may be a device ID or its name; if a name matches more than one, it reports the ambiguity rather than guessing.

callout3.title: This address is for agents
callout3.text: The {'@'} mention menu in the pane input lists local panes only (including those in other windows on this machine), and has no button for inserting a cross-device address. Cross-device addresses are written on the agent's to: line, or sent by an MCP tool (see the "Agent collaboration" topic). When delivery fails the reply is device-offline, unknown-target, link-offline or link-unauthorized; note also that reply threading does not cross machines.

s5.p11: The first block on Settings ▸ Navide Cloud is called Sync. It is not a separate tab — it is the top section of this one page. Each syncable scope gets a row with a toggle; turn one on and that scope stays the same on every device signed in to the same account. Records are encrypted on this machine, and the server only stores ciphertext it has no key for.

sync.scopes: Six rows, one per Agent Assets page and in the sidebar's order; three can be turned on: MCP (the servers you added in Navide; their secrets are encrypted before they leave), Skills (which skills are on and which CLIs each one goes to, plus the files of skills created in Navide; skills you put in the folder yourself sync their settings only) and Prompts (prompt skills and the loop prompt).
sync.credentials: Memory, Credentials & keys and CLI extensions are listed but greyed out, and their line reads "not syncable yet". This is not "off by default, waiting for you to turn it on" — the toggle does not move. A Memory or Credentials switch an older build left on can still be turned off.
sync.states: Two states are spelled out under the block: not connected (scopes you turned on catch up once the link is back) and this device has no sync key yet (nothing is uploaded until it has one). There is also a Sync now button, enabled only while connected.
sync.key: The sync key is shown as the first 8 characters of its id, never as the key itself. Rotate key takes two clicks: the first turns it into Rotate now and adds a Cancel beside it. Rotating retires the current key, re-seals every synced record under a new one, and hands the new key to your other devices the next time they exchange keys — it is the move for a key you think has leaked.
sync.legacy: Adopt for this account appears only when this device holds a sync key from before accounts were bound and this account has no key yet. It is a one-time choice: without adopting it you cannot read what was synced under that key, and minting a fresh key instead would leave those records permanently unreadable.
sync.conflicts: When two devices change the same item, neither side is overwritten. It is listed under "Needs your decision" with both versions side by side, and you press Keep this one or Keep theirs. A credential conflict shows only which slot it is (vendor / slot), never the contents.

s6.title: Menus, standalone windows and schedules

cloud.value: Opens the account window (section 5 of this page).

pipeline.value: The management interface for Pipelines and Roles.

resource.value: The resource management interface (section 7 of this page).

standard.value: Standard macOS window actions. Zoom maximizes the window frame and has nothing to do with the font size of pane content.
standard.label: Minimize / Zoom / Bring All to Front

turnStats.value: Opens the Turn Stats dialog (section 8 of this page).

tokenMonitor.value: Opens the Token Monitor, a standalone window (section 8 of this page).
tokenMonitor.label: Token Monitor

s6.note1: Pipeline Manager, Resource Manager and Turn Stats are dialogs opened inside the main window, not separate operating-system windows; Token Monitor is the one that really is a standalone native window (1200×800), and closing a workspace window does not take it with it. None of these Window menu items has a shortcut.

pipeline.p1: Two tabs. Under Pipelines, one flow is made of several stages; a stage takes an ID, a title, a Sentinel (its end marker, e.g. ---DONE---) and whether to Pause for user answers. Every stage carries at least one slot, and a slot needs an Agent, a Role Key, a display name and a Kickoff Body (the opening prompt); it can also be marked 🎯 Designate as global manager — such a slot becomes a cross-stage coordinator once it has finished its own work, and one flow may only have one. A built-in flow you have broken can be restored with Reset to factory stages (it confirms first, and cannot be undone).
pipeline.p2: The Roles tab manages the roles themselves (Key, Label, a one-line summary, System prompt) and notes that changes only affect panes opened afterwards. Both tabs offer ⬇ Export JSON / ⬆ Import JSON / ↺ Reset to Defaults.

helpMenu.github: Navide on GitHub and Report an Issue… — open the GitHub project and its issues page.
helpMenu.shortcuts: Keyboard Shortcuts — opens the Shortcuts tab in settings. This menu item shows no shortcut; from the keyboard it is the chord ⌘K ⌘S.
helpMenu.legal: Six legal pages, in order: Privacy, Security Policy, Code of Conduct, Boundaries, Licenses and Legal, each opening the matching page on navide.dev. (There are no terms of service, and that is deliberate.)

callout1.title: The View menu is missing a few things on purpose
callout1.text: Electron's built-in whole-window zoom (Zoom In / Zoom Out / Actual Size) was removed, because Navide has two zoom axes of its own: ⌘= / ⌘- / ⌘0 change the terminal content font size, and ⇧⌘= / ⇧⌘- / ⇧⌘0 change the interface scale (Settings ▸ Appearance ▸ Interface Scale). Left in place, the native roles' accelerators would fire ahead of both. ⌘R was also changed to "rebuild the focused pane", and reloading the whole window moved to ⇧⌘R, with a Reload Window item in the menu that carries no shortcut. ⌘W is reserved for "close tab" on macOS, so closing a window is left to the traffic lights or ⌘Q.

s6.p1: This machine's background schedules are listed in a tab in the right slot, named Schedule (🗓), and it can be moved to the top or bottom slot. It is not a window opened from the Window menu. Navide's own jobs, your crontab and the macOS launchd jobs share one list: first Up next: the rows whose next run can be computed exactly, in time order, and below a thin Fixed interval divider the rows that repeat every few minutes or on a schedule with no exact time, shown as their interval rather than a clock time, most frequent first; then Always on / on demand and Disabled, folded by default. On Linux only the crontab source applies; on Windows only Navide's own jobs are listed — Task Scheduler already manages the machine's tasks.

crontab.actions: Every row can be disabled, enabled and removed

agents.actions: Only your own entries in ~/Library/LaunchAgents get ⏸ / ▶ and a ⋯ menu; system-level ones are shown without buttons

s6.p2: The system level is read-only because touching it needs root, and Navide never asks for it — the backend blocks it too, not just the interface. Daemons in particular can usually only show their state as State unknown (requires root). Every row expands to show Schedule / Command / Raw line, or Label / Scope / Plist path / Last exit code / State. Remove sits in each row's ⋯ menu; removing a LaunchAgent unloads it and permanently deletes its plist, and asks for confirmation first.
s6.note2: There is no "run now" and no "reveal in Finder" here, only disable/enable and remove. Above them are Rescan and the time of the last scan.
s6.h4: The other windows opened from the UI

editor.how: ⌘⇧I, or click a file in the explorer, in search results, or a file link in the terminal (see the "Code workflow" topic)

git.how: Open in New Window in the Git panel header, or ⌘⇧G

diff.how: Click a file row in the Git panel, or a file inside a commit

branchDiff.how: The branch comparison action in the Git panel

plan.how: Click a plan document path printed in the terminal, or open an HTML plan document; one per workspace

draggedGroup.how: Drag a tab from the top out of the window and drop it; Merge back in the title bar merges it in again (see section 5 of the "Workspaces & panes" topic)

draggedWorkspace.how: Drag a workspace row out of the sidebar (the window needs two or more workspaces)

callout2.title: Two things that are easy to misread
callout2.text: Git History has no window of its own — "View full history" opens the history view inside the Git window. ⌘⇧D no longer opens a window either; it simply switches the left sidebar to the Plans tab. To open the Plan window, start from a plan document itself.

s6.note3: When a workspace is already open in another window, Navide does not open a second copy — it brings that window to the front.

s7.title: Resources and upkeep
s7.p1: Two entry points onto the same data: the resource pill in the status bar (a small panel) and Window ▸ Resource Manager (the full interface). They list the CLIs on the whole machine, not just this window's.

resource.columns: The columns are Name, Trend (a sparkline of the recent trend), CPU and Memory. Idle is shown by the colour of the dot before the name — there is no text label.
resource.totals: Above them are the CPU and memory totals, each with a line for "how much of this machine that is", plus Refresh.
resource.filters: Filter by All / Running / Idle, and sort by Memory / CPU / Name.
resource.actions: Each row has exactly two actions: clicking the name jumps to that pane (and closes this interface), or Reclaim reclaims it. There is no force quit.
resource.autoReclaim: A line underneath states the current auto-reclaim setting (on/off, after how many minutes), with Settings next to it to jump straight there.
resource.disk: The third card at the top, Disk, and the Storage section below come from the same scan (see the next part); the scan only runs when you press Scan, never automatically when the interface opens.

s7.note1: The numbers cover the whole process tree. Reclaiming a busy pane is skipped with Still busy — reclaim skipped.; a pane that has already been closed reports That pane is no longer open.

callout1.title: Memory is a startup floor, not something that grows
callout1.text: An idle CLI still holds the memory it needed to start, often 200–300 MB each. That is a startup cost and it does not shrink because you "restart it periodically" — a restart simply pays the same floor again. The only thing that actually gets the memory back is reclaim: end the process, the pane becomes a placeholder card that continues on one click, and the conversation is picked back up from the CLI's own transcript (see section 3 of the "Workspaces & panes" topic).

s7.p2: The Storage section below the process table in the Resource Manager (click the heading to expand or collapse it). It scans how much disk this app, each CLI's home directory, and the workspaces you have opened take up — 25 items in four categories, 17 of which can be cleaned.

storageTable.examples: Examples of what is in it

appData.value: Rotated backend logs, the current log, the Navide database, settings backups, runtime scratch, the CLI quota cache

electron.value: Chromium caches, downloaded update packages, browser state

cliHomes.value: Archived CLI profiles, profile caches, CLI conversation history, orphaned pane home directories

workspaces.value: Orphaned and stale agent logs, pipeline history and run logs, plan history

s7.p3: Every item is marked with a risk level, Safe / Caution / Danger, and anything untouchable is marked Not removable; Paths expands to show the actual paths. The Stale threshold in the header (7 / 30 / 90 days, 30 by default) decides how long something must go untouched before it counts as stale and becomes cleanable.
s7.p4: Two cleanup buttons in the header: Clean safe items clears every safe item at once; Clean selected clears the ones you ticked. Both show a confirmation stating roughly how much space will be freed, with an extra warning when a Danger item is ticked.

callout2.title: Deleted is deleted
callout2.text: The confirmation button reads Delete permanently — not "move to Trash". There is exactly one item that really needs Clean selected: CLI conversation history (each CLI's conversation history), the only item that is both marked Danger and cleanable. Once it is gone, those conversations cannot be resumed.

orphans.leftover: Leftover CLI processes — when ⚠ N leftover appears in the status bar, clicking it asks "Found N leftover CLI process(es) from a previous run — they can exhaust memory. Clean them up?", with Clean up to clear them and Dismiss to skip. These are processes the previous run did not clean up.
orphans.backend: Backend — clicking the Backend pill in the status bar shows the address and PID plus two buttons: Restart (Start while disconnected) and Stop (only while connected). Restarting the backend takes every CLI process with it; to have conversations resume automatically once it is back, turn on Resume sessions after a backend restart on the General tab.
orphans.timeout: When the backend errors out because it starts too slowly, raise Backend Startup Timeout (15–120 seconds) on the Appearance tab.

memory.where: Resource Manager ▸ Reclaim; or lower the idle threshold under Settings ▸ General

disk.where: Window ▸ Resource Manager ▸ Storage ▸ Clean safe items

leftover.symptom: ⚠ N leftover in the status bar

stubbornKey.symptom: One key will not change no matter what
stubbornKey.where: Check whether it carries a ⚠: keys claimed by the menu cannot be changed here

remoteAgent.symptom: An agent on another machine cannot get through
remoteAgent.where: Settings ▸ Navide Cloud ▸ the rules card (deny by default)

background.symptom: Something is running in the background

moveSettings.symptom: Settings need to move to another machine
moveSettings.where: Settings ▸ General ▸ Settings management ▸ Export Settings Bundle

tokenSpend.symptom: Wondering which turns the tokens went to
tokenSpend.where: Window ▸ Turn Stats; for this machine's whole Claude history, Window ▸ Token Monitor

s8.title: Usage: Token Monitor, Turn Stats and quota cycles
s8.p1: Three surfaces show usage and they are easy to mix up, so start with which is which: they read different data, cover different scopes, and open from different places.

tokenMonitor.where: Window ▸ Token Monitor, its only entry point; it opens as a standalone native window
tokenMonitor.scope: The Claude history on this machine, scanned from session transcripts. No account dimension.
tokenMonitor.label: Token Monitor

turnStats.where: Window ▸ Turn Stats, the ui.window.openTurnStats command, or the ≡ button on the TOKENS panel — three entry points to the same dialog inside the main window
turnStats.scope: The transcript of one pane you pick, scanned live, with an account filter and the CLI version of every turn

quotaCycles.where: No entry point of its own: pick an account under the Accounts heading in the Turn Stats sidebar and it replaces the right-hand side
quotaCycles.scope: That account's quota windows — spend per cycle, peak %, whether it ran out — plus monthly and yearly roll-ups
quotaCycles.label: Quota cycles

s8.p2: The window is titled Claude Token Monitor, 1200×800, and is one scrolling page with no tabs. Its subtitle states the boundary outright: local Claude history · account attribution unknown. It covers Claude only; other CLIs are not here.

tokenMonitor.controls: Two dropdowns at the top: days (14 / 30 / 90) and model (all, or one). Refresh sits beside them and is disabled while the backend is not connected.
tokenMonitor.stats: Five figures: turns, total tokens, mean per turn, median per turn, mean output per turn. A line under them gives sessions scanned / available and when the data is from.
tokenMonitor.comparison: An output comparison of the last 7 days against the 7 before: sample counts, means, medians and a percentage change. It needs at least 10 turns in each period and a nonzero baseline, otherwise it says the samples are insufficient. The page notes that this only describes an observed change — effort and task difficulty are unknown, and a decline does not establish that an allowance was cut.
tokenMonitor.charts: Five per-turn trend charts. The accent line is the trailing 10-turn mean and the gray one is each turn; the horizontal axis is turns in chronological order, equally spaced — not elapsed time.
tokenMonitor.table: A table of local Claude turns, 100 rows per page: time, session (first 8 characters of the id / turn index), model, each token column, and calls.
tokenMonitor.quota: At the bottom, quota scatter plots grouped by reset window, one figure per window. The percentages are provider-reported; the page states that the horizontal axis is "samples in recorded order" and that local tokens cannot be converted into an allowance ceiling. With no samples yet it tells you to enable Claude usage polling in settings and leave Navide running — past limits cannot be reconstructed from token logs.

callout1.title: This window has no account dimension, on purpose
callout1.text: The subtitle says it: account attribution unknown. It scans the Claude session transcripts on this machine, and those sessions may belong to different accounts; the quota samples cover only the profile slot active while Navide was running, and a slot is not a verified account identity. For a per-account view, go to Turn Stats. And when the scan was truncated or hit read errors, the page raises "partial history" and locks the output comparison rather than handing you a percentage computed on half the data.

s8.h2: Turn Stats (a dialog in the main window)
s8.p3: The left side lists panes grouped by workspace, each row naming its vendor and workspace and possibly carrying a quota pill or a ⛔ limit marker. CLIs that report no token usage (antigravity, cursor) are greyed out rather than hidden, with "no token usage" on hover, and a placeholder that was never started reads "not started". At the bottom of the list is an Accounts section (see the next part).

turnStats.columns: The right side is that pane's per-turn table: time, prompt, In / Cache R / Cache W / Out / Total, calls, plus an Account and a Version column. The header says whether the figures are exact or inferred — inferred means cut at turn-end signals, where a long tool call can be split into two turns.
turnStats.account: An account chip filter sits above the table (including "All"), each chip with its turn count; picking one makes the table subtotal per account. Turns that cannot be attributed are listed under Unknown, and the screen says plainly that turns from before the pinned records existed cannot be matched to an account — it does not invent one.
turnStats.version: The version column and collapsed version chart compare observed local tokens across all recorded session turns, with sample counts. These different populations do not establish a price change. Click a bar to filter the table.
turnStats.export: Export CSV includes the version column, and Rescan re-reads the transcript. The failure messages are deliberately specific: no session to read yet, the transcript is no longer on disk, no reader for this CLI, or the pane was never started.

s8.note1: ⛔ marks the turn during which the most recent quota limit was detected. Only that one hit is kept per pane, and detection polls every 5 seconds, so it can land one turn late. Also, do not read the tokens figure in the CLI footer as a running total — it is the context size; Claude re-reads the whole context every turn, which is why Cache R dwarfs the other columns.
