s8.p4: Pick an account under the Accounts heading and the right-hand side switches from the per-turn table to that account's quota cycles, headed by its vendor and whether it is active. Three tabs: Cycles, Monthly, Yearly.

quotaCycles.tabs: The Cycles tab picks a window kind with chips: the rolling five-hour one is the chip labelled Session (5h), and the others are weekly, weekly-model (one model only), monthly and cycle. Which chips appear depends on which window kinds this account actually has.
quotaCycles.cycle: The compact cycle table shows scheduled dates, state/evidence, observed peak, local tokens and the first limit observation. Select a row for breakdown, coverage, formulas, exact timestamps and reconciliation. CLI evidence can precede a 100% reading; legacy sources remain unverified. Missing detail is a gap, not zero. Five-minute local slices do not prove provider capacity.
quotaCycles.periods: Month and Year retain complete UTC calendar buckets. Range filters offer 30/90 days or custom dates; tables/charts show 50 records per page, while summaries and CSV cover the entire range. Completed-cycle averages require trusted evidence and available local detail. All-account shares refer only to observed local activity; missing components do not imply a complete total.

callout2.title: The account dimension has a start date, and the screen says so
callout2.text: Saved and historical identities remain reachable without open panes, including removed profiles. Unattributed records remain in the separate Unknown bucket; they are never assigned to Default by guesswork. History is read locally, and retry does not enable disabled polling.

s9.title: Security: Navide Guard and terminal command protection
s9.p1: Settings ▸ {nav} manages two gates. Both are fixed code, never an AI.
s9.p2: Guard grades each risky CLI action as {critical}, {high} or normal, then handles it by where the request came from: you at this computer, a chat app, another pane or device, or a pane that has taken in outside content. The decision table at the top is fixed; requests approved from a chat are refused at high and above.

items.builtin: {builtin}: each rule can be set to {critical}, {high} or "{off}". Raising takes effect at once; lowering or turning off needs a confirmation, and eight floor rules (reading or sending credentials, Keychain, download-and-run, deleting root or home, formatting, raw disk writes) can go no lower than {high}.
items.branches: {branches}: force-pushing or deleting these branches is {critical}; terminal command protection's force-push check uses the same list. Removing a branch needs a confirmation.
items.rules: {rules}: each is "{deny}" or "{allow}". A deny pattern raises matching commands to the level you choose; an allow pattern can lower {high} to normal (never {critical}) — that is what an exception is; there is no separate exceptions list. Adding an allow or removing a deny needs a confirmation.
items.test: {test}: type a command to see how Guard would grade it.
items.taint: {taint}: a pane that has received content from a chat, a remote device, another pane or MCP shows an "{badge}" badge in its header, and until you clear the mark every {high} and {critical} action it takes is asked at this computer first. The badge opens the log of what was delivered and clears the mark.
items.audit: {audit}: the decisions Guard made most recently.

s9.p3: Plain terminal panes (not CLI agents) refuse destructive commands such as rm -rf / or format C:, reading each line the way every shell would. Here you can switch categories on and off (turning one off needs a confirmation, turning one on does not), add "{block}" and "{allowEx}", and try a command in "{termTest}".

git.caption: The top half of the Git panel: the commit area, Staged Changes, and Changes. Drawn in HTML, so it follows your theme.

sections.label: Section headers
sections.text: The right end of each header holds the bulk actions: − unstage all, ↩ discard all, ＋ stage all. The number counts the files in that section.

status.label: Status letter
status.text: M modified, A added, D deleted, U untracked, ! conflicted. The grey text after a filename is its directory.

commit.label: Commit area
commit.text: The ✦ beside the message box has a CLI write the commit message; the ▾ next to Commit holds commit-and-push, amend and the rest.

conflict.caption: ConflictPane: one conflict block at a time, rather than the whole file either way.

head.label: Title strip
head.text: The CONFLICT chip, the file path, and how many blocks are resolved out of how many. The Base toggle brings the common ancestor into view.

choices.label: Four choices per block
choices.text: Accept Ours, Accept Theirs, Accept Both, or Edit it yourself. Turning Base on adds an Accept Base button.

apply.label: Apply & Stage
apply.text: Only clickable once every block is settled; it writes the result back and stages the file in one go. This button is in English regardless of the selected interface language — that is what the product prints.

diff.caption: DiffPane: the single-file diff a click on a file row opens, side by side.

hunk.label: Hunk header
hunk.text: The {'@'}{'@'} line says which lines of the original this block covers. A file has as many headers as it has changed regions.

sides.label: Two columns
sides.text: Old on the left, new on the right. A row with only one side filled is a plain deletion or a plain addition.

actions.label: Per-hunk actions
actions.text: Stage, unstage and discard all work on this one block rather than the whole file. They disappear when you are looking at a commit, because history is read-only.

sample.message: fix(git): keep the hunk selection after a stage

codeWorkflow.intro: The Git panel, plan documents, the built-in editor and preview — everything you need to see what the agent changed, review it, and get it committed. It reuses the workspace/pane vocabulary.

s1.title: The three work surfaces
s1.p1: Once an agent has finished changing code there are three things left to do: see what it changed, decide whether to keep it, and move the plan forward. Navide has a surface for each; every one of them works as a sidebar tab and can also be opened as a separate window.

git.title: Git (Source Control)
git.text: The tooltip reads Git (⌘4). In the main window ⌘⇧G opens the separate Git window directly; so does Open in New Window in the panel header.

plans.title: Plans (plan documents)
plans.text: The ⌘5 tab is only a list. Clicking any entry pops up a separate Plan Review window titled <project folder> — Plans.

ide.title: Mini-IDE (the built-in editor)
ide.text: Open it with ⌘⇧I, or click a file in Explorer. The title is <file name> — Mini-IDE, prefixed with ● while there are unsaved changes.

callout.title: All three windows carry the same AI Terminal
callout.text: The Git window, the Plan window and the Mini-IDE each have a narrow rail along their right edge; open it and you get the AI Terminal — a real CLI agent pane (not an API chat window) where you can pick an agent and use Start, Interrupt and Stop. It injects the current context (workspace path, the open plan, the selected code) into the agent automatically, so you can read a diff and tell it what to fix at the same time.

s2.title: Git: staging and committing
s2.p1: The panel is titled SOURCE CONTROL and is split into Staged Changes and Changes (turning on Show Ignored Files adds an Ignored section as well). Click a row to open its diff; ⇧ or ⌘ click selects several, and a "N selected" label plus an ✕ appears above.
s2.p2: To the right of a section header sit the whole-section actions: Staged Changes has only a − (Unstage All Changes); Changes has ↩ (Discard All Changes) and ＋ (Stage All). Right-clicking a section header adds Save Draft on top of that.

callout.title: List mode is one button short
callout.text: In View as Tree a folder row carries its own ＋ / ↩ / −, so you can stage or discard a whole subtree. In View as List, however, a staged row keeps only ⊡ — to unstage it use Unstage All Changes in the section header, the context menu, or switch back to the tree view first.

s2.p3: The input placeholder reads Message (⌘↩ to commit), and ⌘↩ submits. The ✦ next to it is AI commit message — it reads what is currently staged and writes one for you (it turns into ⟳ while it runs).
s2.p4: The primary button reads ✓ Commit; the ▾ beside it (More options) opens, top to bottom:

amend.what: Folds into the previous commit; the input placeholder changes to Amend message….

undo.what: Unwinds the last commit back into the working tree.

auto.what: A toggle, with an ON / OFF badge on the right.

s2.p5: With Auto Commit on, the status bar walks through one round: Auto Commit waiting — triggers in {'{'}count{'}'}s → Staging all changes… → Running lint check… → Generating AI commit message… → Committing…. There is no confirmation step anywhere along that path, so think before you turn it on.
s2.p6: The ··· in the header (More options) holds three groups: View as List / View as Tree; Sort by with Name / Path / Status; and Show Ignored Files. Whichever option is in effect is marked with a ✓. List and tree are also exposed as their own buttons in the header.
s2.h4: Folders that are not a Git repository yet
s2.p7: You get a Not a Git repository card offering Initialize Repository, Initialize (without .gitignore) and Initialize in a specific folder…, with a URL field below it for Connect to Remote. If subfolders contain other repos, it lists Found {'{'}n{'}'} Git repo(s) in subfolders; when one workspace holds several repos, a row of repo tabs appears at the top of the panel (the workspace root is marked ⌂, and each tab carries its branch name and change count).

s3.title: Git: branches and remotes
s3.p1: The pill at the very bottom of the panel shows the current branch (a detached HEAD simply reads (detached)) plus the ahead/behind counts; click it to expand the branch panel.

list.create: At the top is the branch creation field, placeholder New branch name…, with ＋ on the right to submit.
list.localRow: Every local branch row carries four buttons: ⇔ Compare, ⇡ Rebase onto, ⇣ Merge into current, ↵ Switch. The current branch shows only a ✓ and no buttons.
list.context: Right-click a branch row for Merge current branch into {'{'}branch{'}'}, Merge current branch into {'{'}branch{'}'} & push and Delete Branch.
list.remote: ⇅ toggles Show remote branches / Hide remote branches; each remote branch row has a ⬇ Checkout locally.

s3.p2: Pressing ⇔ expands the result inline in the panel, headed {'{'}branch{'}'} ↔ {'{'}current{'}'}, with a stats line and the file list.

account.behavior: Account for this workspace — which Git account this workspace uses. When nothing is bound it reads No account, and the menu lets you pick a saved account or + Add new account….

publish.behavior: Publish Branch. Only shown while the branch has no upstream.

push.behavior: Push, with a superscript in the top right for how many commits you are ahead.

s3.p3: Inside ▾: ↓ Pull, ↓ Pull (Rebase), ↑ Push, ↑ Push (Force with lease); if more than one remote is configured, a Push to remote group is appended at the end with one row per remote.

callout.title: On an auth failure, check the account binding first
callout.text: When a push fails, look at which account the account pill is bound to before you start resetting the remote. When credentials expire the panel points you straight at Settings › Accounts to renew them. The password field wants a Personal Access Token, not your login password.

s4.title: Git: conflicts, drafts and history
s4.p1: While a merge, rebase or cherry-pick is in progress a banner appears at the top of the panel reading ⚠ {'{'}op{'}'} in progress plus the number of conflicted files, with an Abort {'{'}op{'}'} on the right. There is also a dialog titled Merge conflict ({'{'}count{'}'} file(s)) offering the two routes Abort merge and Resolve conflicts. Once everything is resolved the banner becomes ✓ All conflicts resolved — ready to commit merge with a Go to commit button.
s4.p2: For a plain whole-file decision the ↰ / ↱ on the file row is enough. To work hunk by hunk, open ConflictPane:

conflictList.badge: The title carries a CONFLICT badge with {'{'}n{'}'} / {'{'}m{'}'} resolved next to it.
conflictList.choices: Each conflict hunk offers Accept Ours, Accept Theirs, Accept Both, Accept Base, or Edit to fix it by hand (then Confirm / Cancel).
conflictList.base: The Base toggle brings up the common-ancestor version for comparison.
conflictList.apply: When everything is handled, Apply & Stage writes it back and stages it.
conflictList.binary: Binary files cannot be merged three ways — it simply says Binary conflict and only whole-file decisions are available.
conflictList.agent: The Git window has one more button, Resolve with agent, which hands the whole conflict to a CLI agent.

s4.p3: Navide calls a stash a Draft; the card sits in the lower half and reads No draft when empty.

draftList.save: Saving one: right-click the Changes section header → Save Draft, or right-click a single file → Save File as Draft. The dialog is titled Save as Draft (label optional) and the label may be left blank.
draftList.restore: Getting it back: three buttons per row — ⎘ Apply (keep stash), ↑ Pop (apply & remove), ✕ Drop.

s4.note: There is no toolbar button for this, only the context menu — not finding it the first time is normal.
s4.h3: Seeing changes: four kinds of diff

file.what: DiffPane: one file's working tree / staged / a given commit's differences, with per-hunk Stage, Unstage and Discard. Read-only when viewing a commit.

branch.how: ⇔ on a branch row, or Diff Review in the Mini-IDE header
branch.what: BranchDiffPane: a whole-branch comparison, file list plus side-by-side hunks, with an AI Review toggle and Expand All / Collapse All. Diff Review always opens a new window.

inline.what: Expands two nested sub-panels in place: this file's commit history, and below it the diff plus blame. It does not open a window.

history.how: View full history on the History card

s4.p4: The History card in the panel draws its own SVG swim-lane graph with the HEAD dot highlighted. The Git History window is the full table: five columns, Graph / Description / Author / Date / Commit, switchable between All branches and Current Branch, Date order and Ancestor order, plus Show Remote Branches, with Search commits… above and Load more below. Right-click any commit for Checkout (Detached), Create Branch…, Create Tag, Merge into current, Cherry-pick, Revert, Reset Current Branch to This Commit…, Copy Commit ID and Copy Commit Message.

callout.title: AI Review flows into Problems
callout.text: The notes produced by AI Review in BranchDiffPane are not just shown alongside the diff — they are written into the editor's diagnostics, so the same batch shows up in the Mini-IDE's Problems tab (⌘⇧M) where you can jump through them one by one.

s5.title: Plan documents: the list and the lifecycle
s5.p1: Plans do not all live in one folder. Navide scans seven directories under the workspace: .agent-team/plans, .agent-team/reports, .claude/loop-reports, .claude/plans, .cursor/plans, docs/plans and docs/reports — plus the same seven inside any nested Git repository at most two levels deep. Three suffixes count: .html, .plan.md and .md. An HTML plan is named <kebab-slug>_<6 hex digits>.html, a Markdown plan <kebab-slug>.plan.md. Files beginning with an underscore or a dot (_spec.md, _template.html) are scaffolding and never appear in the list.
s5.p2: These files are written and updated by agents — every action you take in the plan window (changing a todo's status, leaving a review note, approving) lands back in the same file. Your part is to ask an agent to "create a plan for me" and then review it in the window.
s5.p3: The sidebar Plans tab (⌘5) and the left column of the Plan window use the same list. The toolbar only appears once there is at least one plan:

listTools.search: The Search plans… field, matching title, file name and overview.
listTools.stage: Stage filter: All stages / Draft / In Review / Approved / In Progress / Done / Abandoned.
listTools.sort: Sort by: Title, Last updated or Progress, with ↑ / ↓ next to it for ascending or descending.
listTools.group: ☰ switches between "group by stage" and a single flat list.

s5.p4: All four choices are remembered per workspace. The sections, top to bottom: Recent (5 at most, pinned ones first); then — grouped by stage — a Documents section plus one section per stage, which a flat list collapses into a single All plans; then Archived; and at the bottom a completed-actions row (Archive all done / Delete all). Every row carries its stage pill, a {'{'}done{'}'}/{'{'}total{'}'} done progress bar, a HTML / Markdown format tag, and {'{'}count{'}'} for you — the items only you can clear. Every row also has a pin 📌 and a delete ✕ on its right (archived rows get the delete only).

callout1.title: Documents without metadata get their own section
callout1.text: When the list is grouped by stage, plain documents that carry no plan metadata collect in a Documents section and each row is tagged Document — which has nothing to do with whether a stage is in-progress. To turn such a file into a real plan, right-click it and choose Promote to Plan: that adds a draft plan envelope and does not rewrite the body.

s5.p5: Right-click a row, top to bottom: Open in editor, Copy path, Select, (HTML only) Rename and Share to Git, (plans only) Archive / Unarchive, (plain documents only) Promote to Plan, Delete. Open in editor is the only entry that hands the file to an editor — clicking a row itself opens the Plan window and never replaces the editor tab you have open. A rename must match kebab-slug_6hex.html or it is refused. A plan row can also be dragged straight onto a CLI pane to hand that agent the goal.
s5.h3: Stage and archived are two different things
s5.p6: The lifecycle is draft → in-review → approved → in-progress → done, with abandoned as a side exit.

callout2.title: Two independent axes
callout2.text: stage answers "how far has this got"; archived answers "do I still want to see it in the list". archived is a flag, not a stage — an in-progress plan can be archived, and a done plan can stay in the list.

s5.p7: And one hard rule: an agent only starts writing code once the stage has reached approved (or later). So what the word "start" actually means is: push the stage to approved.
s5.h4: What it looks like once opened
s5.p8: Clicking any row in the list pops up a separate Plan Review window: the plan list on the left, the document in the middle, the AI Terminal on the right. A workspace only ever has one such window — clicking another plan while it is open changes the page in that window instead of opening a second one.
s5.p9: The document body is routed by format: HTML under .agent-team/plans/ gets the interactive preview (a sandboxed iframe where you can edit sections in place, comment on a section, and click a todo to change its status); Markdown with metadata gets PlanMarkdownBody (editable sections, toggleable todos, rendered mermaid); Markdown without metadata is read-only, and so has no toolbar.

s6.title: Plan documents: the review toolbox
s6.p1: The toolbar across the top of the Plan window is the same for both formats: on the left the stage pill, the Archived pill (only while archived) and the {'{'}done{'}'}/{'{'}total{'}'} done progress bar; on the right a row of icon-only buttons. As the window narrows they collapse into ⋯ in order.

todos.opens: The todo list. Left-clicking a status cycles pending → in-progress → done → pending; right-click is what toggles skipped. Each row offers Edit / Delete, and Add a todo… at the bottom adds a new one.

notes.opens: Review notes. It only appears in the toolbar while some are unresolved (otherwise it hides inside ⋯). A note can be attached to a section — that is what the Comment button next to a section is for. The actions are Edit, Delete and Resolve.

execute.opens: Only shown while the stage is approved. Choose an agent to execute this plan: pick a CLI and the whole plan is handed to it, and the stage moves to in-progress at the same time.

more.opens: Outline / Review Notes / History, plus Share to Git, Open in Browser, Reopen, Archive, Abandon and Delete.

callout.title: Two reasons Approve will not press
callout.text: It only lights up while the stage is draft or in-review and every review note is resolved. The disabled tooltip says exactly that: Requires draft or in-review stage with all notes resolved. Note also that draft goes straight to approved — there is no "submit for review" button in the toolbar.

s6.p2: Two more items inside ⋯ are worth calling out:

moreList.outline: Outline — one row per section heading; click one to scroll to it. Only present when the document has headings.
moreList.history: History — past snapshots, newest first, each row with a Preview (opens the old version read-only, with Back to current plan above to return) and a Diff (lists the differences from the current version in place: how the stage changed, which todo changed status, how many were added or removed, how many review notes differ, how many lines were added or removed).

s6.note: Replies to review notes are written by the agent; the interface only reads them. You leave the note and press Resolve, and the agent fills in the reply.
s6.h1: The AI Terminal on the right
s6.p3: When you start a new agent, Navide feeds it first: the workspace path, the plan file currently open, its name, stage and the status of every todo, and the plan content itself. So you can ask "what are the risks in phase three of this plan" straight away, without pasting the file again.

s7.title: The editor window
s7.p1: Open it with <kbd class="cwh-kbd">⌘⇧I</kbd>, or click a file in Explorer. A tabbed Monaco editor, with <kbd class="cwh-kbd">⌘1</kbd>…<kbd class="cwh-kbd">⌘9</kbd> to switch tabs (out-of-range numbers land on the last tab).
s7.h1: The four sections in the left rail

search.note: Search across files; ⌘⇧H replaces across files.

scm.note: The embedded version of the Git panel, with a change-count badge.

problems.note: The diagnostics list, with an error-count badge; AI Review notes land here too.

s7.note1: This section is called Source Control, not Git — inside the Mini-IDE ⌘⇧G focuses it, while the same combination in the main window opens the separate Git window.

goto.action: Go to line / symbol in file / symbol in workspace

multiCursor.action: Multi-cursor: add one above or below

sendSelection.action: Send the selected code to the AI Terminal
sendSelection.note: (while the cursor is outside the editor area)

s7.note2: Replace deliberately avoids <kbd class="cwh-kbd">⌘H</kbd>, leaving that combination to macOS's "hide window". Every shortcut can be changed under Settings ▸ Shortcuts, and <kbd class="cwh-kbd">⌘K ⌘S</kbd> opens the cheat sheet.
s7.p2: If you would rather not use the built-in editor, change the routing under Settings ▸ General ▸ Default editor. The options, in order, are Mini-IDE (built in) (the default), System default application, Visual Studio Code, Cursor and Custom command…. Anything that cannot be detected is greyed out and marked as not installed, with Re-detect next to it to rescan.
s7.p3: Custom command… takes an argv, executed directly rather than through a shell; the available placeholders are {'{'}file{'}'}, {'{'}dir{'}'}, {'{'}line{'}'} and {'{'}workspace{'}'}, and three ready-made templates are supplied. Left empty, files still open in the Mini-IDE.

callout.title: On macOS, code / cursor are not on PATH by default
callout.text: Having VS Code or Cursor installed does not mean the code / cursor commands work — that is a separate step you have to do by hand. Navide checks PATH first and falls back to looking in /Applications/<App>.app/…/bin/. If launching really fails it falls back to the Mini-IDE automatically and shows an Editor unavailable notice once (once per session per editor).

s7.p4: Three kinds of open always go to the Mini-IDE regardless of this setting: diffs and branch comparisons (there is no file on disk to hand over), an empty open with no file specified, and opens started from search or the Git sidebar.

s8.title: File preview and the change record track
s8.p1: Navide decides how to open a file from its file extension alone (the decision has to be made before the content is read). Anything not in the table below opens in the text editor.

image.ext: png jpg jpeg gif bmp webp ico svg avif apng
image.how: The image, with Fit to window / Actual size.

video.ext: mp4 webm mov m4v mkv ogv

audio.ext: mp3 wav m4a ogg flac aac opus

html.how: A sandboxed iframe, labelled sandboxed · no scripts. Opens on the source by default; switch with Preview / Raw.

csv.how: A sortable table, up to 5000 rows. Also opens on the source by default.

archive.how: Lists the archive contents in two columns, Name / Size.

notebook.how: Cell by cell, up to 500 cells.

office.how: Converted by the backend, then displayed.

binary.ext: gz bz2 xz 7z rar jar war exe dll so dylib bin dat o a class pyc wasm db sqlite sqlite3 dmg iso eot doc xls ppt pptx
binary.how: An info card plus a hex dump of at most the first 64 KB.

s8.p2: Markdown is not in this table; it takes another route: .md uses MarkdownPreview, but .plan.md is routed to the plan view.

callout1.title: Only html and csv do not preview automatically
callout1.text: Every other kind in the table opens straight into the preview; html and csv deliberately give you the source first and only switch when you press Preview. Note also that docx, xlsx, zip and woff are on the binary list as well, but the font, archive and Office checks run before the binary one, so they get their dedicated rendering rather than falling back to a hex dump.

s8.p3: The lower half of the right-slot Preview tab (⌘⌥V) is Recent changes — what has been touched in this workspace lately. Four columns per row:

trackList.path: Path — elided in the middle when too long.
trackList.who: Who did it — the agent's name; with no attribution it simply reads —, and never guesses.

s8.p4: Four filter buttons above: All / You / Agent / Watcher. Clicking a row brings that file or diff back into the preview area in the upper half (rows for deleted files do nothing).

callout2.title: It survives closing the window
callout2.text: This record is written by the backend into the workspace's own database (<workspace>/.agent-team/navide.db), keeping the latest 300 entries per workspace, and survives closing the window or restarting the app. It is loaded at app startup, so you do not have to open the right slot first. When the same change is reported once by the file watcher and once by an agent, the two entries are merged into one, with the attributed one winning — so you never see the same thing twice.

s9.title: Shortcut cheat sheet
s9.p1: The keys this book covers. The full list, and how to customise it, is under Settings ▸ Shortcuts.

escape.action: In order: cancel editing / close the menu / leave the snapshot / close the window

fileTabs.action: Switch to the Nth file tab (⌘1…⌘9)

callout.title: The same combination does different things in different windows
callout.text: <kbd class="cwh-kbd">⌘⇧G</kbd>, <kbd class="cwh-kbd">⌘⇧M</kbd>, <kbd class="cwh-kbd">⌘⇧F</kbd> and <kbd class="cwh-kbd">⌘1</kbd>–<kbd class="cwh-kbd">⌘9</kbd> are each claimed by all three windows, so the "in which window" column above is a condition, not a remark. Also, once the AI Terminal inside the Git or Plan window has focus, all these keys go to the CLI and are not intercepted by the window.

s10.title: Plans is a Navide plugin — and what it looks like when it fails
s10.p1: Both the sidebar Plans tab and the Plan window are drawn by the bundled Navide plugin navide.plans, listed under Bundled in Settings ▸ Navide Plugins with its id, version, Active/Removed/Unavailable badge, manifest permissions and package version. Nothing in the interface calls it "v2" — the one exception is the recovery panel below.
s10.p2: Switching the app theme repaints Plans immediately; no window needs reopening.
s10.h1: When Plans cannot start: Legacy recovery
s10.p3: If the Navide plugin fails to start this session, the Plans tab is replaced by a grey Legacy recovery label with the previous plan pane below it, and a line naming the cause: Plans v2 was withdrawn this session ({'{'}reason{'}'}). Reasons you are likely to see: forced (the environment variable NAVIDE_PLANS_RECOVERY=legacy asked for it), storage-migration-failure (the durable storage record could not be read or migrated), and the backend’s own start-up failure text.

list.retry: Retry Plans v2 re-arms the Navide plugin so the next Plans open spawns its backend again. Two attempts per session, and the budget is spent up front: pressing it costs one whether or not it works. Once they are gone the session stays on the legacy pane until you restart the app.
list.repair: Repair storage record appears only when the reason is storage-migration-failure. A successful repair leaves you in recovery and says Storage record repaired. Restart Navide to leave legacy recovery.; a record that was never broken answers The storage record is readable — nothing to repair.

s10.p4: When NAVIDE_PLANS_RECOVERY=legacy forced recovery, or no complete v2 package is registered this session, Retry refuses outright and prints why beside the button — no attempt is spent.

menu.caption: The menu the ＋ on a workspace or group row opens. Drawn in HTML, so it follows whichever theme you use.

role.label: Role picker
role.text: Pick the role first, then the CLI; the role's instructions are injected once the pane is up. Leaving it empty opens a pane with no role.

pick.label: CLI list
pick.text: The ✓ marks the one you used last, which is what ＋ opens next time. The order here is the order of Ctrl+1…9.

missing.label: Not installed
missing.text: A CLI whose binary cannot be found is still listed and still clickable — clicking it opens the guided install rather than a pane.

install.caption: The guided install dialog, stopped on step one, Check.

steps.label: Three steps
steps.text: Check → Install → Verify. A finished step turns into a ✓, and the primary button is always whatever comes next.

chain.label: Installation order
chain.text: When more than one thing is missing the whole chain is listed at once, instead of one failure at a time.

command.label: Command that will run
command.text: Shown verbatim, and only runs once you press the button; the output then appears in the terminal inside the dialog.

settings.caption: Settings ▸ CLI Agents: the card grid, and the launch overrides and permission bypass in the drawer opened for Claude Code.

grip.label: Drag grip
grip.text: Dragging reorders the ＋ menu, and with it which CLI each of Ctrl+1…9 opens. It only works while the filter is "All" and the search box is empty.

toggle.label: Enabled box
toggle.text: Clearing the box only removes the CLI from the ＋ menu; nothing is uninstalled. At least one must stay enabled.

perm.label: Three-state bypass
perm.text: The drawer holds this CLI's row only: follow the global setting, always bypass, or never bypass. The global switch above it is the same one in every CLI's drawer.

launch.label: Launch overrides
launch.text: The drawer shows this CLI's fields directly; there is nothing to expand. A red "Not passed through" means Navide manages that variable itself, so the value never reaches the CLI.

usage.caption: The quota badge in a pane's header, expanded on hover.

windows.label: Quota windows
windows.text: One CLI can have several windows at once — a five-hour one and a weekly one, say — and each gets its own bar.

reset.label: Reset time
reset.text: When this window goes back to full. A ～ in front of a figure means it is a cached reading, not a fresh one.

accounts.label: Account switch
accounts.text: CLIs that support several sign-ins can be switched right here; switching swaps credentials without killing running panes.

cliAgents.intro: How the supported CLI agents are installed, tuned and given multiple accounts, and where quota and cost figures come from. Settings ▸ CLI Agents shows agent cards; Manage opens Overview, Launch, Permissions, Push, and Install sections together on one scrolling page. Launch decides which command line a newly spawned pane starts on. Terms (workspace, pane, group) follow the "Workspace & Panes" topic.

s1.title: Supported CLIs
s1.p1: The table lists the built-in CLI agents. The order below is the default order of the + menu and of <kbd class="cah-kbd">Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd class="cah-kbd">1</kbd>…<kbd class="cah-kbd">9</kbd> (drag to reorder in Settings, see chapter 4).
s1.note: "Quota" = Navide can read the remaining usage (chapter 6). "Multi-account" = several sign-ins can be kept in Settings and switched (chapter 5). The four CLIs without a permission-bypass flag (Grok CLI, OpenCode, Pi, MiniMax Code) simply have no such flag — it is not something Navide left out. "Sign-in command" = what Navide actually runs when you press Sign in under Settings ▸ Accounts; the CLIs marked "Inside the CLI" declare no separate sign-in command, so the button launches them as usual and signing in happens on their own screen.

callout.title: The 16th entry is not an agent
callout.text: >_ Open Terminal at the bottom of the + menu is a plain shell: no agent is attached and no role is injected. It sits deliberately outside the list so the CLI list's scrolling never hides it.

s2.title: Install & detection
s2.p1: Navide never downloads or installs a CLI itself. It only runs each vendor's own command, and always shows you the full command before it runs.
s2.h1: What a missing CLI looks like
s2.p2: In the + menu and the Manual spawn agent dropdown, vendors whose binary is not detected get a suffix: Kimi Code — not installed. Nothing else changes — not greyed out, not disabled — the entry can still be clicked.
s2.p3: Detection is throttled to 10 seconds and refreshed at these moments: the backend connects, the + menu opens, the Manual spawn agent dropdown receives focus.
s2.h2: What happens when you click one
s2.p4: Clicking a CLI marked as not installed makes Navide re-detect first (you may have just installed it elsewhere). If it is still missing, no doomed pane is opened — the guided install dialog appears instead. There are exactly three ways it appears: the pane exited with 127, the backend’s pre-launch probe reported the binary missing, or you picked a CLI that is not installed from the + menu or Manual spawn yourself. It no longer lands on top of a pane that would in fact have started.
s2.p5: Three entry points share one dialog; only the source differs:

spawn.when: You picked a CLI that is not installed from the + menu or Manual spawn.

pane.when: The pane actually opened but the CLI was not found — the PTY exited with 127; or the backend's pre-launch probe reported the binary missing (covers Open Agent, ↻ Resume, a pane opened by the issue-handling flow, and pipeline stages).

settings.when: You opened that CLI's drawer in Settings ▸ CLI Agents and pressed "Install" in its last part, "Installation and updates" (the button only appears while the CLI is missing).

s2.p6: The dialog always has three steps: Check → Install → Verify.

steps.check: Check: shows installed / not installed / outdated and how many steps this Mac needs (for example a numbered Homebrew → Node → CLI chain). Prerequisites that cannot be installed automatically are listed separately. "Command that will run" is shown verbatim.
steps.install: Install: the command runs in a terminal embedded in the dialog, where you can watch the output and answer its prompts (password, sign-in). A chain continues into the next step by itself.
steps.verify: Verify: once a version is detected, shows ✓ and the binary path. Only when it was opened from a pane (pane) is there an extra "Start {'{'}CLI{'}'} again" button that reconnects the pane that just died.

s2.p7: Only one install dialog exists at a time — a pipeline that makes five panes of the same CLI exit 127 together does not stack five dialogs.

callout.title: "Not now" is not "stop asking"
callout.text: Closing the dialog or pressing Not now remembers nothing; it will ask again next time. To really silence it, tick Stop asking about {'{'}CLI{'}'} at the bottom. That tick only blocks the automatic pop-up (pane died, pre-launch probe failed); when you pick that CLI from the + menu yourself the dialog always opens — you asked for it. The tick is recorded per vendor and kept forever, until you untick it; it never expires.

s2.h4: Installed but will not start: how PATH is searched
s2.p8: A CLI installed with npm -g, nvm, volta, pnpm or bun used to be invisible to the backend’s PATH probe when Navide was launched from Finder, and the spawn was refused before the pane even opened — which read as "it runs in my terminal but not in Navide". A probe that finds nothing no longer blocks; the pane’s own login shell gets to look again. A --version that exits non-zero but still prints a version now counts as installed too; only printing no version at all is treated as missing.
s2.p9: One ordering trade-off on macOS: nvm’s version directories now sit after your own PATH rather than in front of it, so Navide no longer quietly replaces the node you picked with nvm use. If you were (unknowingly) relying on Navide to put nvm’s node first, you now get whichever one your shell PATH names. On macOS pnpm’s home is ~/Library/pnpm.
s2.h5: Being signed out is called out too
s2.p10: The pre-launch probe is a --version smoke test: it can answer "is it installed", not "is it signed in". So when a spawn finds evidence that a CLI is signed out, Navide says so up front instead of letting the pane sit silently on the vendor’s own sign-in screen. The test is deliberately "evidence of being signed out", not "evidence of being signed in" — vendors whose credential files Navide cannot inspect are never reported, because a false "not signed in" on every one of them would be worse than silence. No notice therefore does not mean you are signed in.
s2.p11: The guided install dialog gained an outcome to match: when the binary is there but no account is behind it, the last step reads "{'{'}CLI{'}'} is installed, but not signed in", with an explanation, the binary path and a Sign in button — which opens a pane that runs the sign-in for you, after which most CLIs open your browser. (The first-run setup wizard itself gained no sign-in step; it is still Environment, Agents, Permissions, Ready.)

callout2.title: Grok CLI is now xAI’s official one
callout2.text: It installs from the vendor’s own script (curl fetches https://x.ai/cli/install.sh and hands it to bash) rather than from npm — so it needs curl and a real Terminal window. The update command is grok update, and the config file is now ~/.grok/config.toml, with MCP written as TOML; the community build’s user-settings.json is no longer read. It has no diagnose command (the vendor ships none, so Settings links the official docs instead), no effort field and no permission-bypass flag. The same-named community CLI installs to the same path, so which grok cannot tell them apart — only the shape of the version string can.

s3.title: Roles
s3.p1: A role is one system prompt plus an id, a name and a one-line summary. Those four fields are all there is — a role is not tied to a CLI, carries no colour and no flags.
s3.p2: Five default roles are built in: pm, backend, frontend, mobile, qa.
s3.p3: The Roles tab of the Pipeline Manager window (menu Window ▸ Pipeline Manager). The role list is on the left, the four fields on the right. You can add, delete, reset to defaults, and export / import JSON.
s3.note: Editing a role does not affect panes already running — the editor says so right underneath: "Changes apply to new spawns only". The Settings window only reads the same role list; it has no editor of its own.
s3.h3: How a role is applied when a pane opens
s3.p4: The top of the + menu and the Manual spawn dialog each have a Select role… dropdown; both share one selection. Manual spawn can also expand a preview of the role's summary and full prompt.
s3.p5: The mechanism is plain: the role's system prompt is pasted into the CLI's input box as if you typed it, then Enter is pressed. No flag is changed and no config file is written. What is actually pasted is the role prompt plus a fixed standby suffix (asking the agent to reply "ready, awaiting task" and stop), plus the pane's session marker.
s3.p6: During this stage the pane status reads injecting role. Before injecting, Navide automatically dismisses the CLI's startup trust dialog (by sending one Enter) and waits for the screen to settle.

callout.title: A plain terminal has no role
callout.text: A plain terminal opened from the + menu carries no role. The reason is the sentence above: a role is text typed into the CLI prompt, and a shell would just echo it back.

s3.p7: Reapply role in the pane's context menu is only enabled while the pane is running and was spawned with a role. It pastes the role prompt once more — no CLI restart, no conversation reset.
s3.p8: Two differences from the first injection: this time the bare role prompt is pasted, without the standby suffix or the session marker; and if the pane has a kickoff prompt, it is sent again automatically 3 seconds later.

s4.title: Settings ▸ CLI Agents
s4.p1: The tab opens on a grid of cards, one per CLI. To adjust one, click anywhere on its card or on {manage} ›, and that CLI's own settings drawer slides in from the right. Launch overrides, permission bypass, push channels and installation and updates, which used to be laid out down one page, now all live in that drawer, one CLI at a time.
s4.p2: Above the grid sits a toolbar: a search box ({search}, matched against the name), three filter buttons {all} / {enabled} / {attention}, and {redetect}. A line below it counts how many CLIs are shown, how many exist and how many are enabled. Each card has an {enabledBox} box at the bottom that decides whether the CLI appears in the + menu and the Manual spawn dropdown; at least one must stay enabled, so the last box locks. Drag the ⠿ in a card's top-left corner to reorder — that order also decides which CLI Ctrl+1…9 maps to — but only while the filter is "{all}" and the search box is empty; otherwise the count line says "{reorderFiltered}".
s4.attention: A ! beside a card's name means "{attention}". Any one of four things sets it: the CLI is not installed, it is outdated, it is detected as signed out, or the environment check has a finding about it. The "{attention}" filter lists exactly these cards.
s4.p3: Most CLIs have a flag that skips their permission prompts so the agent runs unattended. The setting has two layers:

list.global: A global switch at the top: Bypass permission prompts by default (YOLO mode). Every CLI's drawer shows this same switch, so changing it in any one changes it for all.
list.perVendor: Below it, one row for this CLI, showing its actual flag (for example --yolo) with a three-way dropdown on the right: Follow global / Always bypass / Never bypass.

s4.p4: For the four CLIs without a flag (Grok CLI / OpenCode / Pi / MiniMax Code), this part of the drawer shows only the global switch, with a line below it saying that this CLI has no bypass flag and there is nothing to switch.

callout1.title: Changes do not reach running panes
callout1.text: The flag is written into a pane's command line the moment it starts. Changes here only affect panes spawned afterwards; a running pane keeps what it started with until you rebuild or restore it.

s4.h3: Also: Model and Effort in the Manual spawn dialog
s4.p5: Four CLIs (Claude Code, Kilo Code, OpenCode, Qwen Code) can be handed a message directly instead of having it typed into their input box. Each has its own switch in its drawer, beside a line stating that vendor’s cost (a local port with no password, a local port with a per-pane password, a plaintext temp file, a background hook). For every other CLI this part of the drawer is a single line: no push channel is declared, so messages arrive as ordinary terminal input. Changing one updates every open window at once. Details are in the "Inter-CLI Messaging" and "MCP" topics.
s4.p6: The last part of the drawer covers this CLI only: a status badge (installed / not installed / outdated), the version, the install method (npm / Homebrew / official installer / official install script), the full binary path, and the outcome of the last update (success or failure, when, and from which version to which). Available actions:

update.detail: Runs the vendor's own update command in the embedded terminal below this part, where you can watch the output and answer its prompts. Vendors without an official command get an "Update via vendor docs" link instead.

doctor.detail: Runs the vendor's doctor command in the same embedded terminal.

install.detail: When the CLI is missing, opens the guided install dialog from chapter 2. When it is installed, the button becomes "Reinstall (command)" and reruns the vendor's install command in the embedded terminal, to repair a CLI that is installed but misbehaving.

autoUpdate.detail: Keep the vendor default, or switch to manual (update only from here).

redetect.detail: One sits in the toolbar above the card grid and one beside this part's heading in the drawer; both force a fresh scan.

s4.p7: When several physical installations of one CLI are detected, an extra list appears with every path, marking the active one; for the others you can press Use this one to switch, or Remove — which, unlike updates, opens a separate external terminal to run the vendor's uninstall command.
s4.note: Updates replace the binary; panes already running must restart to pick up the new version.

callout2.title: What is not here
callout2.text: There is still no "default arguments" field — a launch command replaces the line rather than appending to the default. The binary is still not chosen by typing a path, but by picking one of the candidates when several physical installations are detected (after which the drawer's overview gains a "Custom binary" chip). Model and reasoning effort, though, are no longer MCP-only: launch overrides has proper fields for them, and so does the Manual spawn dialog.

s4.chipsIntro: A card shows only three chips: install status, sign-in and accounts, and push channel. The full strip sits in "{overview}" at the top of the drawer and reads back how that CLI is currently set up. The order is fixed, and follows "what it is → what it runs as → how it is reached":

install.shows: Installed (with version) / update available / not installed. Nothing is drawn while a CLI has not been probed yet — "not asked" is not "not found", and is never painted red.

model.shows: "model …" and "effort …" appear only once you have chosen one under launch overrides; the vendor default gets no chip. CLIs that cannot be told which model to run at launch always show "No model flag".

permission.shows: Permissions inherited / forced on / forced off. Not drawn for the CLIs with no bypass flag.

push.shows: push (with its kind) / push off / no push.

account.shows: Signed out, or how many accounts are attached. Not drawn for CLIs whose sign-in state Navide cannot read.

binary.shows: You picked one of several physical installations rather than the default.

command.shows: This row has a launch command set. It is deliberately amber, because it also switches off the model and effort above it.

env.shows: How many environment variables this row adds.

s4.chipsLegend: The colours are consistent: green = normal or on, amber = a deviation worth noticing, red = unusable or switched off, grey = a neutral fact.
s4.drawer: The drawer is titled with the CLI's name and detected version. It holds five parts, top to bottom — {overview}, {launch}, {perm}, {push}, {install} — on one scrolling page, not as tabs. "{overview}" repeats the full chip strip and the same {enabledBox} switch. While the drawer is open the card grid behind it is inert; close it with ✕, a click on the dimmed area outside it, or Esc, and focus returns to that card's {manage} ›. Every change is saved as you make it; there is no Save button.
s4.drawerSearch: Settings search opens the drawer too: a launch, permission, push or install result opens the CLI named in your query; with no name, the one you managed last, and failing that the first one it applies to (a permission result only picks a CLI that has a bypass flag).
s4.launchIntro: This part decides which command line a newly spawned pane of this CLI starts on. The drawer only holds this CLI's fields, so there is nothing to expand. Everything here is per CLI and per machine, not per project, and applies to every window. The chips at the top of the drawer show what has been changed (model, effort, custom command, how many env).

model.detail: A free-text box (empty = vendor default). Model ids change with every vendor release, so this is not a dropdown. Only CLIs that can be told a model at launch have this field.

effort.detail: A dropdown for the vendors that publish a closed list of levels, a text box for the rest. A combination the vendor cannot honour is refused on the spot and not saved, naming the values it does accept.

command.detail: Empty = use the default. Fill it in and you are writing the whole line — see the warning below.

env.detail: One row per variable and value, add or remove at will. A name may only use letters, digits and underscores and may not start with a digit (a name with a space or an equals sign cannot go into a process environment at all).

callout3.title: A launch command means Navide adds nothing
callout3.text: This is the easiest thing to get wrong here. The moment the launch command is non-empty, the default model and effort above it, the permission-bypass flag and any per-pane argument are all left off — the line runs exactly as you wrote it. The one thing that still applies is the custom binary (a separate setting), and it only replaces the leading token: a wrapper line such as npx claude does not start with claude, so nothing is swapped. Clear the field and everything above comes back.

s4.launchResume: Two other paths ignore this setting. Rebuilding a pane, or restoring one after a restart, has to rebuild the resume command from the vendor’s own syntax, so those panes launch on the default command. A login pane is the same: the backend keeps only the first token of the command and appends the vendor’s sign-in subcommand, so a wrapper line would become something like npx auth login. Navide cannot merge the two — it has no way to know where a session id belongs inside a line you wrote.
s4.launchReject: Asking for a model at the same time is refused outright rather than silently dropped. When an agent opens a pane through MCP, a request naming a model or effort for a CLI that has a custom launch command is rejected with the reason (a resume is the exception — its command is rebuilt from the vendor’s syntax and never reads this setting). The reasoning: a pane that quietly fell back to the default model looks exactly like one that got the model you asked for.
s4.launchEnv: The environment table has a reserved list of names Navide manages itself (the full current list is printed verbatim under the section, and that is the one to trust). A reserved name is not forbidden: you can still save it, the row just gains a red "Not passed through" — and it starts working the day Navide stops managing that variable. The dropping happens at spawn time, and the window that asked for the pane gets a notice. There are two kinds: denied (the value never existed in the pane’s environment at all) and superseded (it went in, then a higher-priority source of Navide’s own rewrote or deleted it — it looks applied and is not). Neither stops the pane from opening.
s4.launchEnvNote: The reserved list is global, not per vendor — setting CODEX_HOME on the Claude Code row is refused too. It grows and shrinks with what Navide manages, so do not memorise the count; read the list printed under the section.
s4.spawnIntro: The Manual spawn dialog gained a Model and an Effort field, prefilled from whatever that CLI has under launch overrides (re-read each time the dialog opens, never cached). Model is free text; Effort is a dropdown whose options come from the levels that vendor publishes. Which fields appear is not a hard-coded list — it follows whether the vendor spec declares the matching launch argument:

both.vendors: Claude Code, Antigravity CLI, Copilot CLI, Muse Code, Pi

modelOnly.vendors: Codex, Cursor CLI, Grok CLI, Kilo Code, Kimi Code, OpenCode, Qwen Code

neither.vendors: Aider, Droid, MiniMax Code, and Terminal (which is not an agent)

s4.spawnNote: The seven "Model only" CLIs are not short of a reasoning knob; the knob just is not a launch argument. For some it is baked into the model id (a trailing -high, say), for others it lives in a config file or behind an in-session command. A value that breaks the rules (a model id containing a space, or starting with "-") is explained on the spot and disables the submit button. And if that CLI has a custom launch command, both fields are disabled with the reason spelled out — that line runs as written and Navide adds no model to it.
s4.pushAllOff: Turning them all off is a valid choice; there is no "keep at least one" rule here. With all four off, the drawer's push part lists three costs: messages wait until the receiving pane is idle and are then typed into its input, so they arrive later; Claude Code's rewake is the only way to wake an idle agent, so without it you wait for the agent to go idle on its own; and panes already open keep the channel they started with until they restart.

s5.title: Accounts
s5.p1: Settings ▸ Accounts holds two unrelated things: Git accounts in the top half, CLI accounts in the bottom half.
s5.p2: All 15 vendors get a heading, but only 5 support multiple accounts: Claude Code, Codex, Kimi Code, Grok CLI, Kilo Code. The rest print one line — "This agent does not support multiple accounts." — with no add button at all.
s5.p3: Under each vendor the first card is always the built-in Default (your original login credentials); the accounts you added follow. A card shows the signed-in email, the Default tag and that account's remaining quota.

add.detail: Creates a profile, then opens a temporary login pane that launches the CLI's browser sign-in. Once authorised, the account shows as signed in and the pane closes by itself.

login.detail: Shown only when the account is not signed in or its credentials expired.

setDefault.detail: Switches the active account. While switching, the button reads "Switching…" and every account's buttons are temporarily disabled.

refreshQuota.detail: Only the account the CLI is currently signed in as can be read.

delete.detail: Confirms in place. Removes the stored credentials as well.

s5.note1: Every account can be renamed, the built-in Default included: hover a card and click the pencil (the same pencil sits on each row of the quota badge's account list). The name you give it leads everywhere — the pane header, the account list and the cards — with the signed-in identity kept below it. Clear the field to go back to the generated name (Account 1, Account 2…).
s5.p4: Two cases refuse deletion and say why: the account is currently active (switch to another one first), or its sign-in is still running (finish or close its login pane first).
s5.p5: What happens to running CLIs when you switch? Navide does not kill them. The default is to refuse the switch and tell you "N running CLI pane(s) are using this account — close them before switching." If you insist, a confirmation appears: Switching accounts will restart N running {'{'}CLI{'}'} pane(s). Continue? After "Switch & restart", those panes are rebuilt with resume (reconnecting the original conversation), not killed. If any pane fails to rebuild, a summary notification appears.
s5.p6: Claude Code is the exception: it re-reads its credentials before every request, so the switch is a hot swap — no confirmation and no pane restart.
s5.p7: Switching too often is blocked (at most 3 times per 60 seconds per CLI); confirming a forced switch does not bypass this.

callout1.title: Open panes keep the previous account
callout1.text: The panel says it itself: "already-open panes keep the previous account until reopened". All accounts share your real home directory (sessions and history are shared); switching accounts swaps the stored credentials in place.

s5.h2: Sign in outside Navide and it notices
s5.p8: If you run claude /login or similar in your own terminal, Navide's credential watcher is watching each CLI's credential directory. About 0.8 seconds after a file changes it reads an "identity fingerprint"; if the fingerprint is unchanged nothing happens, otherwise the "Default" pointer moves to the matching account and a quota re-read is triggered. The email, Default tag and quota badge on the Accounts panel update live.
s5.p9: If the live credentials match no registered account, Navide creates a profile for that email automatically. Nothing touches your credential files and no pane is restarted.
s5.note2: Limitation: if a CLI has never signed in (its credential directory does not exist yet), watching only starts after Navide is relaunched.
s5.p10: Four fields: Label, Host (default github.com), Username, Token. Each row in the list shows host · username · ••••last four — the token itself is never returned to the UI. Leaving Token empty while editing keeps the old one.
s5.p11: Tokens are encrypted with the OS keychain (safeStorage) and stored locally; decryption happens only in the main process. When the keychain is unavailable a yellow notice appears, the add button is hidden entirely and editing is disabled.

callout2.title: Binding is done elsewhere
callout2.text: "Which Git account this workspace uses" is chosen with the account pill on the Git panel in the sidebar. The Settings page only adds, edits and deletes accounts. Deleting an account also clears any binding that pointed to it.

s5.portable1: Account cards gained a Portable credential field: run the vendor’s own command to obtain one and paste the result in. Today only Claude Code declares a portable credential (the command is claude setup-token); the other thirteen have no such field. What you paste is encrypted on this machine and handed to newly spawned panes through their environment — it is never written into the CLI’s own credential files.
s5.portable2: The card shows Not set or Set, and when the credential is outranked it says so plainly — "not in effect", naming what ranks above it — because most CLIs put their own login file, a key helper or an administrator’s policy directory ahead of the environment. To make a pasted credential take effect, sign out of the CLI there first.
s5.portableNote: The card also carries marks such as "From cloud" and "In use"; those belong to credentials that arrived through cloud sync. Navide Cloud’s Credentials scope is currently listed but not switchable, so reusing a credential pasted on another device is not reachable yet — what you paste stays on this machine.
s5.switchToast: A failed switch is now always visible. Only two refusals used to raise a toast — "panes are running" and "switching too often". Everything else, a failed credential swap included, went into the Accounts panel’s own banner, which had long scrolled out of view while you were looking at one vendor’s rows; pressing "Set as default" looked like nothing happened at all. Every kind of switch failure raises a toast now.

s6.title: Quota display
s6.p1: The quota badge lives in the CLI pane's title bar (not the status bar) and shows the remaining percentage; hover to expand the details — each metering window, reset times, and the account switcher. The account cards in Settings ▸ Accounts read the same data.
s6.p2: 11: Claude Code, Codex, Kimi Code, Grok CLI, Antigravity CLI, OpenCode, Qwen Code, Kilo Code, Pi, Copilot CLI, Cursor CLI. Aider, Muse Code, Droid and MiniMax Code have no readable quota source.

list.claude: Claude Code is special: Navide never touches its credentials; it runs claude -p /usage and reads the quota report the CLI prints itself. Each read therefore starts a full Claude Code and takes a few seconds.
list.others: The other 10: Navide reads the credentials that CLI already keeps on this machine and queries the vendor's own usage API. Read-only — refreshing the token is always left to the CLI that owns the file.

s6.note: Apart from a few vendors with an official query path, most CLIs have no official "check quota" command; Navide uses each vendor's usage endpoint. Anything it cannot read is shown honestly as "unavailable" — nothing is guessed or filled in.

percent.meaning: Normal. Hover for reset times and the per-window breakdown.

reading.meaning: You just switched accounts and the new account's quota is being read. Claude has to start its CLI once — up to about a minute; the previous numbers stay until then.

cached.meaning: This read failed; the numbers are from the last successful read, with its time.

expired.meaning: Credentials expired — re-login in that CLI.

cliMissing.meaning: The binary is not on PATH, so nothing can be read and there is no cache to fall back on.

limit.meaning: The CLI itself reported it is out of quota. With no readable reset time it just says "out of quota". This badge can be dismissed — see below.

s6.p3: The badge switch and refresh interval are in Settings ▸ General (not the CLI Agents tab). The "Refresh: …" line in the details says why this read did not update: no credentials, credentials expired, rate limited, unavailable, Not measured, failed. When it failed, a "Reason: …" line underneath gives the actual error instead of leaving you with a bare "unavailable".
s6.p4: When the CLI prints its own out-of-quota message, the pane gets a ⛔ badge with a countdown to the reset (or just "out of quota" when no reset time can be read), and a notification goes out. This is a different thing from the percentage badge above: the percentage is what Navide queried, this one is what the CLI said.
s6.p5: The badge can be clicked away. The confirmation warns you first: if a loop is waiting for the quota to come back, dismissing it resumes the loop now. The dismissal only holds until that particular reset (matched with a 60-second tolerance, because each poll re-resolves the reset against its own clock), and expires with it — hitting the limit again the next day counts as a new event even if the clock time reads identically. The dismissal is also tied to the account that ran out: switching to another account keeps it suppressed, switching back to that one lifts it. When no reset time can be read there is no suppression at all (with no clock there is nothing to tell an old banner from a new hit by), and the badge is cleared instead by a five-hour fallback.

s7.title: Idle reclaim & CLI cost
s7.p1: Every running CLI holds a block of memory that is allocated at startup and never released — the Settings page puts it at "often 200–300 MB each". With a dozen panes open, that becomes a whole-machine problem.
s7.p2: So by default Navide demotes panes that have been quiet too long to a placeholder: the process ends, but the slot, name and messaging address all stay, the card reads Click to resume, and pressing it brings the conversation back from the CLI's own transcript.

list.threshold: The threshold is 15 minutes / 30 minutes / 1 hour / 3 hours / 8 hours / Never (default 30 minutes), in Settings ▸ General.
list.exempt: The focused pane, a pane awaiting your answer, and a pane with unsent text in its input box are never reclaimed.
list.now: The same section has a Reclaim now button that first tells you how many panes qualify and roughly how much they hold.

s7.note: The full reclaim behaviour (including what a placeholder looks like) is in the "Workspace & Panes" topic; per-pane CPU / memory figures and the Resource Manager window are in "Settings & System".

notInstalled.symptom: The pane exits immediately, or the + menu shows "— not installed"
notInstalled.cause: The binary is not on PATH (the PTY exited with 127), or the pre-launch probe could not find it.
notInstalled.fix: The guided install dialog opens by itself; follow the three steps, and at Verify press "Start {'{'}CLI{'}'} again" to reconnect the pane. If you ticked "Stop asking" earlier, the automatic pop-up is off — pick that CLI from the + menu instead; that path always opens the dialog.

notDetected.cause: It may need a new terminal session, or it landed outside PATH.
notDetected.fix: The dialog says so directly. Go to Settings ▸ CLI Agents and press "Re-detect". If several physical installations are listed there, use "Use this one" to pick the one you want.

loginExpired.cause: The CLI itself printed a login-expired message. Only Claude Code and Droid have this detection today.
loginExpired.fix: Click the badge; Navide sends that CLI's login command into the pane. The badge clears only after the injection succeeds; on failure it stays lit so you can click again.

parkedExpired.symptom: After switching, an account says "Not signed in" or its token expired
parkedExpired.cause: The token expired while that account was parked.
parkedExpired.fix: Navide starts a sign-in on its own and posts a notification explaining why. That is the normal result of parking an account too long, not the switch breaking something.

detectingSession.symptom: The pane sits on the "detecting session ID" overlay
detectingSession.cause: The CLI has not written its session file yet — usually because it is stuck on a screen that needs your answer (a first-run API key prompt, a trust dialog).
detectingSession.fix: The overlay has a 30-second grace period, then lifts by itself so you can use the terminal directly — detection keeps running in the background. The subtitle keeps saying "detecting session ID"; that is normal. Aider has no session id and never shows this overlay.

quotaStale.symptom: The quota display does not update
quotaStale.cause: You just switched accounts (Claude has to start its CLI once — up to about a minute); or this read failed and the cache is shown; or that CLI has no readable quota source at all.
quotaStale.fix: Check the "Refresh: …" line in the badge details first — it states the reason. To re-read immediately, press "Refresh quota" at the top of Settings ▸ Accounts (it skips the wait after a failed read). Note that only the account the CLI is signed in as can be read; parked accounts only show the cache.

panesRunning.symptom: "N running CLI pane(s) are using this account — close them before switching."
panesRunning.cause: Non-Claude CLIs do not allow the credentials to be swapped in place while a pane is running.
panesRunning.fix: Close those panes and switch again; or choose "Switch & restart" in the confirmation so Navide rebuilds them with resume. Switching too often is blocked by the 3-per-60-seconds limit — wait a moment and retry.

permissionFlag.symptom: Changed permission bypass, running panes do not react
permissionFlag.cause: The flag was fixed into the command line when the pane started.

notOnPath.symptom: It runs in my terminal but will not start from Navide
notOnPath.cause: The backend’s PATH probe could not see a binary installed by nvm / volta / pnpm / bun / npm -g, and refused the spawn before the pane opened.
notOnPath.fix: A probe that finds nothing no longer blocks; the pane’s own login shell looks again. If it still fails, press "Re-detect" in Settings ▸ CLI Agents. Note that on macOS nvm’s directories now sit after your own PATH, so the version you picked with nvm use is no longer replaced by Navide.

signedOut.symptom: The pane opens straight onto the CLI’s own sign-in screen
signedOut.cause: The CLI is installed but signed out — the pre-launch probe can only tell whether it is installed.
signedOut.fix: Navide announces this first; the last step of the guided install dialog also has a Sign in button that opens a pane and runs the sign-in for you. Vendors whose credential files Navide cannot read are never reported, so the absence of a notice does not mean you are signed in.

launchCommand.symptom: A default model is set but the pane did not use it
launchCommand.cause: That CLI also has a custom launch command. The line runs as written, and Navide adds no model, effort or permission-bypass flag to it.
launchCommand.fix: Clear the launch command, or put the model into the line yourself. An agent asking for a model through MCP is refused with the reason; in the Manual spawn dialog both fields are disabled.

envIgnored.symptom: An environment variable set under launch overrides had no effect
envIgnored.cause: It is on the reserved list Navide manages itself, or it went in and was then overwritten by a higher-priority source.
envIgnored.fix: The notice raised at spawn names the variables and which case they fell into: denied = it never went in, superseded = it went in and was then rewritten or deleted. The reserved list is printed under the launch-overrides section. A name that is not on the list and is still superseded usually lost to credential or CLI-home management, which writes after your request.

resumeIgnoresCommand.symptom: After a rebuild or a restore the pane ignored my launch command
resumeIgnoresCommand.cause: A resume command has to be rebuilt from the vendor’s own syntax, and Navide has no way to know where the session id belongs inside a line you wrote.
resumeIgnoresCommand.fix: This is deliberate, not a fault. If you need those arguments, go back to the vendor’s default command and set them through the default model and effort fields instead.

s9.title: CLI risk observations
s9.p1: A small pill starting with ▲ can appear in a CLI pane's title bar, after the login-expired and usage-limit badges. It is invisible by default — it shows only when Navide has observed one of the three situations below, and only the most severe finding at a time (red before yellow). This is not a settings feature: there is no switch for it anywhere in Settings; you only ever meet it on the pane:

network.when: The pane's process tree (the CLI itself, its MCP servers and tools) holds an established TCP connection to an IP outside that vendor's declared host set. The set is built by resolving the vendor's declared hostnames (cached for 5 minutes) plus anything you have allowed. Only Claude Code and Codex declare hosts today; every other vendor reads "Unsupported". Any proxy or base-URL environment variable disables the comparison outright. TCP only — no UDP/QUIC — and macOS and Linux only; Windows is unsupported.

disk.when: A file appeared in that vendor's data directory (~/.claude, ~/.codex and so on) that is larger than 100 MiB and whose first 64 KiB Navide cannot recognise (SQLite, archives, PDF, images, GGUF and plain text are all recognised; a file extension alone never counts). Only files first seen within 24 hours, and only after a first baseline scan exists — anything already there is never flagged. Aider declares no data directory, so it is not scanned.

diskAgain.when: A path that was flagged before was confirmed absent and then observed again in the same 100 MiB size class. Once red, it stays red.

s9.p2: Clicking the pill opens a "CLI observations" dialog listing every finding for the pane with its evidence (vendor, endpoint or path, connection count or size, each observation time, observation status, last successful sample), followed by a scope line and a caveat. Network findings are scoped to this pane's process tree; file findings apply to every pane of that vendor. Each finding offers:

actions.ignore: Dismisses this finding; it will not be shown again.
actions.ignoreIp: Network only — ignores every port of this IP for this vendor.
actions.allowIp: Adds the IP to that vendor's allow list so it is never flagged again; the decision is stored in this machine's settings and survives a restart.
actions.reveal: File only — shows the file in Finder / the file manager.

s9.p3: Sampling rides on the existing resource poll — there is no separate timer: every 30 seconds while idle, every 2 seconds while the resource window is open. File sweeps are further limited to once per vendor every 5 minutes, at most 100,000 entries and 20 seconds each, and symlinks are always skipped. While the backend is disconnected the pill keeps the last evidence it received and marks it stale.

callout.title: It observes; it never acts
callout.text: Navide never blocks a connection, pauses a CLI or deletes a file on its own — the pill means "something is worth a look", and every line in the evidence dialog says what it can and cannot prove (an observation time is not a creation time; the destination hostname and the traffic content are unknown). Conversely, no pill is not an assurance of safety: it covers only the situations, vendors and platforms listed above.

messaging.intro: A CLI agent inside Navide can hand an instruction to another CLI agent — in the same workspace or in another workspace window. Every CLI pane has a name, and that name is its address: the text you see in the pane's title.

callout.title: The one thing that matters
callout.text: You never have to memorise any syntax. Just say it in plain language — "ask reviewer to run the tests" — and the agent looks the address up and sends it itself. The syntax below is there for when you need to debug.

s1.title: How it works
s1.flow:
pane "architect"             Navide             pane "reviewer"
     │                                                 │
     │  "reviewer, run the tests"  ──►  roster lookup  │
     │                        and is it idle?  ───────►  received, runs it
     │                                                 │
     │  ◄──────────  the reply takes the same path  ◄──┘
s1.p1: A message is sent automatically — it is not pasted into the input box for someone to press Enter; the other side simply starts working.

s2.title: The two routes
s2.p1: There are two ways to send a message. Delivery is identical either way; what differs is how the agent learns it has the ability, and which CLIs support it (see the next section).

mcp.title: MCP tools
mcp.p1: The agent sees them in its own tool list the moment it starts, so nobody has to teach it. It can look up who is online first, then send the instruction.
mcp.p2: The ones it reaches for most (the full list is in the "MCP" topic):

tools.list: List targets — who is online, how their address is written, and whether they are busy right now.
tools.send: Send an instruction — deliver arbitrary text to a named pane.
tools.spawn: Open a new agent and hand it work — ask Navide to open a new CLI pane, choose which CLI it runs, and give it a task. The new pane should report back to the caller with a message once it finishes, but that is the sub-agent's own output, not something Navide guarantees: it queues while the caller is busy, and it never arrives if the sub-agent does not follow the format.
tools.ack: A pure acknowledgement — "got it", "done", anything the other side need not act on. It is written to the message log for you to read (badged "ack only") but is never typed into the other agent's input box, so it neither interrupts nor wakes it — which also means anything the other side has to read or act on cannot go this way.
tools.pending: Check who is waiting on me — a busy pane cannot be typed into, so the agent can ask the question itself: what is queued waiting for it to go idle, and whether anything it sent is stuck.

mcp.note: Ten of the fifteen CLIs are wired to this tool set (see the table in the next section). The ones that are not — Aider, Droid, Muse Code, Pi — use the output protocol below instead; MiniMax Code has neither route yet and can only receive.

proto.title: Output protocol
proto.tag: panes in a pipeline have it automatically
proto.p1: The agent emits a bare text block like this in its reply and Navide picks it up as a message:
proto.code:
---MSG-START--- to: reviewer
Run pnpm test:run for me and report the list of failures back
---MSG-END---
proto.note: to: may sit on the same line as ---MSG-START--- or alone on the line directly below it; any to: further down counts as content. The ---MSG-START--- and ---MSG-END--- lines must start at column one — no indentation — and must not sit inside a markdown code block, or they are not recognised and nothing reports an error. Pipeline slots are told about this protocol in their opening brief; manually opened panes are not, but you can paste the block above straight to one — provided that CLI supports the output protocol in the table below.

s3.title: Which CLIs can send
s3.p1: Every CLI pane can receive messages — Navide types the text straight into the terminal, which has nothing to do with the CLI. Fourteen of the fifteen can also send; only the route available to them differs:
s3.note1: Fourteen of the fifteen can send; only the route differs. The output protocol needs Navide to read that agent's own log — the fourteen vendors that ship a log reader are all covered, so Navide can tell when the agent has finished saying something, and what it said. MCP tools additionally need the CLI to offer a way in (a launch flag, one environment variable carrying the whole config document, or a per-pane mirror of the config directory); Aider, Droid, Muse Code and Pi offer none, so they use the output protocol only. MiniMax Code has neither: it keeps its conversations in SQLite and Navide has no reader for that shape yet, so it can receive messages but cannot send.
s3.note2: Two caveats in practice: Antigravity cannot send on the turn where the agent asks you a question (that turn carries no reply text) — ordinary answering turns are fine; and Qwen, Pi and Kimi have no explicit "turn finished" signal, so Navide infers it from 8 seconds of silence and the send goes out a little later.

s4.title: How to address the other side

pane.meaning: Looks only inside your own workspace

folder.meaning: A pane in another workspace window

device.meaning: A pane on another machine (both must be signed in to Navide Cloud)

list.noSlash: Without a slash it never leaves your own workspace. Crossing projects always has to be spelled out.
list.ambiguous: Not found or ambiguous is always refused — never guessed. Sending an instruction to the wrong CLI is worse than not sending it.
list.broadcast: Broadcast (all) does not cross workspaces. Crossing projects is always a deliberate, named act.
list.device: Copy a cross-device address from the list rather than assembling it. The first segment may be the machine's id or its name, and only the id is guaranteed not to collide with one of this machine's own workspace paths.

s5.title: When the other side receives it
s5.p1: Not immediately. Navide waits until the target is genuinely idle before typing into it, so it never interrupts what it is doing:

list.alive: Its CLI is still alive and past the startup phase
list.noTyping: Nobody is typing in that pane (a draft in the box, or a keystroke in the last four seconds, makes it wait)
list.quiet: No output for the last 2 seconds

s5.p2: If the conditions are not met the message queues; once they are, it goes out automatically. So while the target is on a long task your message waits for it to finish — that is deliberate.
