The Inter-CLI Messages panel names which condition is holding it — "Target pane is not running", "Target pane is still starting up", "Someone is typing in the target pane", "Target agent is mid-turn", "Waiting for the target to settle" — so "it never went out" always has a findable reason. The message the target receives is prefixed with its source, so it knows who to reply to.
s5.note: A few CLIs (Qwen, Pi, Kimi) have no "turn finished" signal in their logs, so Navide cannot tell when they are done and treats "quiet for 8 seconds" as the end instead. Messages to those CLIs may therefore wait a little longer.

list.panel: The "Messages" tab (✉) on the right rail — opens the Inter-CLI Messages panel, showing each message's source, target, status and what is holding it; cross-workspace ones carry an extra "cross-workspace" badge. Anything not yet delivered can be taken back with "Withdraw", a failed one sent again with "Resend", and delivery as a whole stopped with "Pause delivery".
list.crossWorkspace: When a cross-workspace instruction arrives — the target window raises a notice so you know the instruction was not one of yours.
list.mention: Typing {'@'} in the input box — brings up a picker that includes addresses in other workspace windows.
list.drag: Dragging one pane onto another — if the caret sits right after an {'@'} the other pane's address is inserted; otherwise a summary of its screen content is pasted.
list.wake: The "Click to resume" placeholder card — after a workspace is reopened, a pane comes back as a card with no CLI behind it. When messaging one of those, the agent can ask Navide to open it first and then deliver, so you need not click it yourself; if it comes up on a fresh session the reply says so, because that agent remembers none of the earlier conversation.

s7.title: Asking an agent to open another agent
s7.p1: Besides messaging, an agent can ask Navide to open a new CLI pane and assign it a task — useful for splitting work up in parallel, or handing it to a CLI better suited to it. Again you only have to say so in plain language: "open a codex to review this PR".

list.name: The new pane's name is its address, so a role name works best.
list.report: Once the task is done the new pane reports back with a message to the agent that opened it.
list.rejected: A rejection only ever comes from getting the request wrong: no such CLI name, a duplicate or invalid name, an empty task, or a model or reasoning effort that CLI cannot accept.
list.kickoff: Whether the opening task actually went in is reported too. Navide waits for the CLI to boot, for its prompt to appear and for the task to be typed before answering. When it could not confirm delivery it says "check the status first" rather than "resend" — a blind resend dispatches the same work twice.
list.duplicate: A repeated request for the same spawn is blocked, so an agent that gives up waiting and asks again does not end up with a second pane.
list.resume: A new pane can also be opened onto an old conversation. The agent lists the CLI conversations this workspace still holds and names one; the new pane starts with that conversation's memory intact (including one started in a plain terminal). The id is checked against that CLI's own session store first, and an id with nothing behind it is refused rather than quietly opened empty.

children.label: Child panes one pane should open

depth.label: Depth of the spawn chain (a pane you opened opening more)

s7.note: These are guidelines, not hard limits — going over is never blocked, it only attaches a reminder to the reply for the agent to pass on or note, the point being to stop it recursing until the machine chokes. Panes in a pipeline can do the same thing with a ---SPAWN--- block, under the same guidelines.
s7.note2: Resuming a conversation is something you could always do yourself: the manual-spawn card has "↻ Resume", and the Agent History panel has "↻ Resume session". What is new is the agent's side — it can now list the resumable conversations itself.

s8.title: Guardrails
s8.p1: So agents cannot flood each other:

rate.limit: Rate for one source → target pair
rate.why: Two agents replying to each other can loop forever

queue.why: Nothing should pile up without bound while the target is swamped

timeout.why: When the target window is closed, a message must not sit in "Queued" forever

pause.why: You can stop delivery at any time; messages queue instead of going out

noTool.symptom: The agent says it has no messaging tool
noTool.cause: That pane was opened before the feature shipped (MCP tools are wired at pane startup), or that CLI is not one of the ten wired to MCP
noTool.fix: Close the pane and reopen it; if that CLI has no MCP wiring at all (Aider / Droid / Muse Code / Pi), ask it to use the ---MSG--- output protocol instead

staleId.symptom: It reports the pane id as stale
staleId.cause: The pane was detached to another window, or the window reloaded: its identity changed but the CLI still holds the old one
staleId.fix: Reopen that pane; or switch to the ---MSG--- protocol, which uses the current identity every time

unknownWorkspace.cause: No workspace window is open for that folder name
unknownWorkspace.fix: Check the other window is open, or have the agent list the targets it can send to first

ambiguous.cause: Two workspace folders share a name, or one workspace has two panes with the same name
ambiguous.fix: Use the full path; for duplicate pane names, rename one of them

stuckQueued.cause: The target is on a long task and has not gone idle yet
stuckQueued.fix: Normal — wait for it to finish; if it really is stuck, it is marked failed after 30 minutes

rateLimit.symptom: The panel says "Rate limit: at most 5 messages per 60s between the same two panes"
rateLimit.cause: More than 5 messages for one source → target pair within 60 seconds
rateLimit.fix: Usually two agents stuck in a pointless loop — go and see what they are talking about

paused.symptom: Nothing moves in the messages panel
paused.fix: Press "Resume delivery" in the Inter-CLI Messages panel

kickoffFailed.symptom: The agent you sent out never seems to start
kickoffFailed.cause: The pane opened, but the opening task could not be typed in (a CLI still painting its first screen gives Navide nothing to confirm against)
kickoffFailed.fix: The pane is open — do not open it again. Look at that pane: if its input box is empty, send the task over as a message

deviceOffline.cause: All three are cross-device only: the far machine has no connection at all / this machine is not connected to Navide Cloud / this machine has never been set up with Navide Cloud
deviceOffline.fix: Only the first is worth waiting out. For the other two, check the link state in the Navide Cloud window; "Access token rejected" means somebody has to sign in again

list.terminalPane: A plain terminal pane cannot send or receive — only CLI agent panes have a name.
list.receiveOnly: Five CLIs have no MCP tools — Aider, Droid, Muse Code and Pi can only use the bare-line output protocol, and MiniMax Code has not even that: it can receive messages but cannot send. See "Which CLIs can send" above.
list.detached: After a pane is detached to its own window, or the window reloads, the MCP tool route only comes back once the pane is reopened; the output protocol is unaffected.
list.queueFull: When the target's queue is full (10 at most) the message is dropped — but no longer silently: the panel says "The target already has 10 messages waiting", the failure is typed back into the sending pane as a notice, and the sending agent can equally look up what became of its own message. Delivery is still asynchronous, so nothing is known at the instant of sending.
list.noPermission: There is no permission prompt — cross-workspace messaging raises no confirmation dialog, only a notice on arrival. That is a deliberate trade-off.
list.ackLocal: A pure acknowledgement does not cross devices — the relay cannot promise the message stays out of an input box on someone else's machine, so a cross-device ack is refused outright; send it as an ordinary message if it has to travel.

messaging.tip: Tip: give panes role names first ("reviewer", "architect") — the title is the address, and everything afterwards reads much more naturally.

delivery.caption: Both ends of one message. The sending pane is on the left, the receiving pane on the right — Navide types the message straight into its terminal and submits it, so what you see is it already working. The first line is always [Navide MSG] from:, which is how the recipient tells "someone messaged me" from "my message bounced".

envelope.label: What the recipient sees
envelope.text: The source on the opening line, then the message itself, then the reply format — that last line is how the receiving agent knows who to answer.

status.label: The recipient's status
status.text: The pane goes from idle to running the moment the message lands; there is no step where someone presses Enter.

panel.caption: The "Messages" tab (✉) on the right rail. One row per message: source → target, time and status, with an extra "cross-workspace" badge on the cross-workspace ones. Delivery as a whole can be stopped here with "Pause delivery".

actions.label: Title bar
actions.text: "Pause delivery" queues later messages instead of sending them; "Clear log" only clears the display and leaves delivered messages alone.

route.label: Source → target
route.text: A cross-workspace row carries the folder name as a prefix and is marked with the "cross-workspace" badge.

status.label: Status
status.text: "Queued" → "Delivering" → "Delivered". A failed row grows a "Resend" button; one still queued can be taken back with "Withdraw".

sample.body: Run pnpm test:run for me and report the list of failures back
sample.hint: (To reply: first line exactly ---MSG-START--- to: architect …)
sample.preview2: Review done, two issues fixed, tests all green
sample.preview3: Measure the home page load time

s11.title: Messaging across devices
s11.p1: Once this machine is signed in to Navide Cloud, the agent's target list grows a second section of panes on other machines. They are listed apart from local ones because the deal is different: the message travels through the server, so it can fail in ways a local one never could.

list.address: The address has three parts: device / workspace / pane name. Copy it from the list rather than assembling it.
list.works: You can tell it something, ask it something, and wait for it — those all work.
list.notWorks: You cannot read it, interrupt it or close it — reading another pane's transcript, sending an interrupt key and closing a pane all need that pane's own machine, so a cross-device address is refused for all three.
list.offline: A remote pane's busy state is near-live, not live — it is the word the far window last uploaded to the server. There is also a separate offline field, meaning that machine or its window is away right now and what you are reading is the server's last impression of a pane nobody can reach.

s11.note: With no Navide Cloud link the section is absent from the target list entirely — not empty, gone. So "I cannot see my other machine" has two readings: not signed in to Navide Cloud, or signed in and no other machine currently has a pane open.

s12.title: What Navide tells the sender afterwards
s12.p1: Delivery is asynchronous, so "sent" only means Navide accepted the message. The real outcome comes back to the sender three ways:

list.notice: A failure is typed back into the sending pane — as a notice under Navide's own name (badged "system notice"), written only once that pane is idle, so a busy agent is never interrupted by one.
list.stale: Being stuck for more than two minutes also earns one notice — one, so a target that stays busy for an hour does not turn into an hour of noise; the notice names what is holding it.
list.check: The agent can look it up itself — every send hands back a key it can use to ask what became of that message (kept for the last hour). It can also wait a while at send time and have the outcome returned directly.
list.busy: An agent too busy to be told goes and asks — a notice can only be written while the pane is idle, so one that works solidly for an hour receives none. It can check between pieces of its own work whether anything it sent is stuck.

s12.note: There is only a pane to write a notice into when the sender is a local pane; a message sent from an external client has none, so looking it up is the only route.

channels.title: Talking to agents from a chat app ({nav})
channels.p1: {nav} bridges Telegram, Discord, Slack, Feishu, DingTalk, Matrix, Mattermost and iMessage to CLI panes, so you can talk to an agent from your phone. A chat binds to one pane, and binding and unbinding are announced in that chat.
channels.receive: Messages are not fetched on a timer: Telegram and Matrix use long polling, the other platforms keep a connection open, and iMessage reads this Mac's message database every second, so a message arrives almost at once while connected. A dropped connection reconnects by itself, first after about 5 seconds, then waiting twice as long each time, up to 10 minutes. Messages sent while Navide is closed are picked up after a restart on Telegram and Matrix; other platforms are not guaranteed to deliver them.

setup.global: At the top of Settings ▸ {nav} is the master switch, "{global}".
setup.bots: Each platform can hold several bots: the first is marked as the main bot, and once the platform is set up "{botAdd}" adds more. Each bot can be renamed, switched on or off on its own, and removed (which asks first and says how many panes it disconnects), and each keeps its own allowlist, pairing requests and link codes.
setup.quick: For platforms that need a secret (all but iMessage), "{quickAdd}" sets up a new bot: the clipboard is read only when you press the button, a token is pre-filled only if it has the right shape, and the bot is kept only once the platform accepts its credential.
setup.link: Once a bot is connected, a guide under the platform links your own account ("{linkAccount}"): open a Telegram DM or add the bot to a group, add it to a Discord server, open a Slack DM, or on the other platforms get a one-time code to send to the bot. The code works once within 10 minutes; when it expires, cannot be saved, or the backend connection drops, the guide stops and says why.
setup.pairing: A stranger messaging the bot gets a pairing code (valid for 1 hour) that waits under "{pairing}" for your approval; approved people appear under "{allow}".

channels.h2: Binding a pane to a chat
channels.p2: A pane's header has a "{connect}" button. Step one picks the chat, grouped by platform and bot: an existing chat, or a new topic; a chat another pane already uses is marked. Step two confirms how much reaches the chat:

levels.replies: {replies} (preselected for a new binding): only answers messages sent from the chat; nothing you type at the computer is sent.
levels.minimal: {minimal}: adds each turn's result and confirmation prompts.
levels.standard: {standard}: also adds notices of local commands, progress and subagent summaries.

channels.p3: A pane that was bound to the same chat before reuses its last level. Redaction only masks this bot's own credentials; everything else is sent as is, and the dialog says so. Once bound, the header shows a chip with the level, whose menu changes the level and lists child panes. Child panes it opens get their own topic under the same chat automatically, and moving the pane to another chat moves its child topics with it.
channels.h3: Answering CLI prompts from the chat

answer.bare: Permission prompts and questions are posted to the chat one at a time. When only one is open, a bare 1–9, yes or no answers it; with several open, add the id after the answer (for example yes <id>). Any other text gets an immediate hint instead of waiting in a queue.
answer.which: Only Claude Code, Codex and Aider can be answered from the chat; other CLIs, multi-select and free-text questions ask you to answer at the computer instead of showing buttons that do nothing.
answer.never: Permanent choices such as "don't ask again", "always allow" or "allow for this session" are never pressed from a chat.
answer.guard: Requests approved from a chat still go through Navide Guard: anything graded critical or high is refused, and so is anything Guard cannot judge; the chat is told the action needs confirming at the computer.

channels.p4: The titlebar's "{monitor}" button carries a status dot: red when a bot is blocked, yellow while one is reconnecting, green when they are fine, and no dot when no bot is enabled. It opens a list of every pane bound to a chat, where you can jump to the pane or disconnect it; automatic child topics are grouped under their parent binding.

workspace.intro: What the main window's four building blocks — workspace, pane, stage layout and sidebar — are, and how to work with them. This is the first part of the manual; every later chapter builds on the terms defined here.

shell.caption: The five regions of the main window. Drawn in HTML rather than captured, so it follows whichever theme you are using.

titlebar.label: Title bar
titlebar.text: The workspace name sits in the centre; the gear on the right opens Settings.

sidebar.label: Sidebar
sidebar.text: Tab icons across the top (Agents, Pipeline, Explorer, Git, Plans), and under them the workspace → group → pane list.

stage.label: Stage
stage.text: The tab row is the run groups; the grid below holds the panes of the open group.

rail.label: Right rail
rail.text: The right-hand panel, collapsed: History, Tokens, Messages and the rest. Click one to expand it.

status.label: Status bar
status.text: Branch, backend link and resource use on the left; announcements, clock and close-all on the right.

groups.caption: The same panes seen twice: a grid on the stage, a list in the sidebar. Switching tab switches which group you are looking at.

tab.label: Group tab
tab.text: One tab is one group; the number on it counts the panes inside.

add.label: New group
add.text: Opens another group. A pane moves between groups by being dragged onto a tab.

grid.label: Pane grid
grid.text: The panes of the open group. The one with the coloured border has focus.

tree.label: Three levels in the sidebar
tree.text: Workspace → group → pane. A further indent means that pane was opened by the agent above it.

s1.title: Three terms
s1.p1: Navide's main window is made of three layers. Get these three words straight first — every later chapter uses them.

workspace.title: Workspace
workspace.text: A project folder. It is also the starting path for every CLI agent — whichever workspace an agent opens in is its working directory. A workspace's private state (pane records, groups, history, plan documents) lives in .agent-team/ inside that folder.

pane.title: Pane
pane.text: One terminal tile running a CLI agent. It has a name, and that name is its address — other agents use it to send the pane a message. A workspace can hold many panes.

group.title: Run group
group.text: A container that groups panes, matching one tab in the tab bar at the top. Use it to keep the agents working on "one thing" together. Switching groups switches which set of panes the stage shows.

callout.title: How the levels nest
callout.text: A window can hold several workspaces; a workspace holds several groups; a group holds several panes. The sidebar's Agents tab lists them top-down in exactly that order.

s2.title: Workspaces
s2.p1: Before any project is open, the window is a full-screen welcome card:

welcome.browse: Browse… — pick a folder to use as the workspace.
welcome.newWorkspace: New… — choose a location, name the folder, and it opens straight away.
welcome.recent: Below that is the recently-opened list, where frequently used entries can be pinned. Right-clicking an entry offers Open in default editor, Reveal in Finder and Copy path.

s2.p2: Afterwards you can always use the menu: File ▸ Open Workspace… (⌘O), File ▸ Open Recent, or File ▸ New Window (⌘N) for a new window.
s2.p3: You do not need a second window for a second project. In the sidebar's Agents tab, the workspace section header has a ＋ on its right that brings the same picker back; the project you choose is taken into the same window, adding one more workspace header row to the sidebar.
s2.p4: Click that header row to switch the view. The key point: a workspace you switch away from keeps its agents running, its row stays in the sidebar, and only its panes are hidden from the stage for now.

callout.title: What a switch replaces
callout.text: Switching workspaces also replaces the tab bar, the stage, the Git pane, the file explorer, the plan list and the terminal working directory. If a pipeline is running you get a confirmation first. During the switch the stage is covered by a loading card.

s2.p5: If the same folder is already open in another window, Navide does not open a second copy — it brings that window to the front.
s2.h3: Workspace groups (the colored rail on the left edge)
s2.p6: The sidebar's far-left edge carries an 8px-wide colored rail. Hovering it opens a flyout where you can add, rename and delete workspace groups, drag workspaces into a group, or pick All to see everything. This layer is for juggling many projects at once; with one or two projects you can ignore it entirely.

s3.title: Panes
s3.p1: The entry point is the ＋ button — there is one on the sidebar's workspace header row and one on every group header row (the only difference is which group the new pane lands in). Pressing it opens a small menu:

addMenu.role: At the top is the Select role… dropdown — pick a preset role.
addMenu.cliList: In the middle is the CLI list, with the ones that are not installed marked as such.
addMenu.terminal: At the bottom are Terminal (a plain terminal with no agent attached) and Manual spawn….

s3.p2: Manual spawn… opens the full dialog, where you can choose the agent and role, decide whether to add it to the stage, whether to open a terminal alongside it, and paste a session id to resume an earlier conversation directly.

rename.how: Double-click the pane title (double-clicking the badge on its sidebar row works too, or right-click ▸ Rename)

s3.note: An auto-named pane carries a tiny ◦ mark after its title; one you renamed by hand does not.
s3.p3: Right-click a pane or its sidebar row: Focus, Rename, Send message, Interrupt, Reapply role, Remove. Of these, Send message inserts that pane's address into the input box of the pane you currently have focused — the fastest way into cross-pane messaging. A pane with sub-panes below it (▸) also gets a Remove N sub-panes item: it closes only what that pane spawned, leaving the pane itself and every other pane alone.
s3.p4: The ⊟ in a pane's top-right corner minimizes it. Once collapsed, its sidebar row is marked Docked, and expanding that row offers ↑ Restore and Remove.
s3.p5: There is also a third state, the placeholder card: the slot is still there but shows a "↩ Click to resume" card, keeping the title, subtitle and group label. After restarting the app, or after an idle reclaim, a pane looks like this. Click anywhere on the card and the CLI carries on with the same conversation.
s3.p6: Every running CLI holds on to memory and GPU. By default Navide demotes panes that have been quiet for too long back to a placeholder card:

reclaim.default: On by default, with a 30-minute threshold you can change in Settings.
reclaim.scan: It scans every 60 seconds, and the test is "no output and no typing from you".
reclaim.notClose: This is not a close: the slot, the name, the message address and the session are all kept — one click brings it back.
reclaim.exempt: Panes a pipeline is reading, panes with a draft in the input box, panes with messages queued for delivery, and the focused pane are never reclaimed.

s3.note2: When a reclaim happens, the History view's pipeline log shows ♻ reclaimed N idle CLI pane(s) — click to resume.

s4.title: Layout
s4.p1: Four small buttons at the far right of the tab bar decide how panes are arranged on the stage:

sidebar.behavior: The focused pane takes the main area, with a narrow column on the right for the other running agents.

spotlight.behavior: The focused pane on top, the rest as a strip of thumbnails below.

fullscreen.behavior: The focused pane fills the stage, the rest collapse into expandable floating windows.

s4.p2: There is also one behavior you do not select, dual-focus: when exactly two panes are running they automatically split left and right, and the divider between them can be dragged.
s4.p3: With more than one pane, Grid mode shows a row of ratio buttons: ∞ (auto), 2×1, 2×2, 3×3, plus a custom columns × rows pair of inputs (1–9) on the right. Once a fixed size is chosen, panes that no longer fit are paged, with ‹ 1/3 › paging on the right. The dividers between columns and rows can be dragged directly.
s4.p4: The whole window is cut into five slots: up, left, main, right, down.

slots.main: main is always the CLI stage — it cannot be moved or collapsed.
slots.left: left can hold: Agents, Pipeline, Explorer, Git, Plans.
slots.right: right can hold: History, Time, Tokens, Schedule, Messages, Preview.
slots.updown: up and down can take History, Schedule and Messages.

s4.p5: Each slot has its own tab strip and a collapse arrow; collapsed, it becomes a 36px-wide rail (clicking an icon on the rail expands it again). Slot boundaries can be dragged to resize.
s4.p6: The fine-grained controls are in Settings ▸ Layout: one row per view, where you can assign it to a slot, hide or restore it, make it that slot's default tab, or type slot widths directly; there are also toggles for the title bar and status bar and a Reset layout. Three ready-made presets:

focus.effect: Both side slots collapse to rails, leaving the screen to the stage.

bottomPanel.effect: History and Messages move to the bottom horizontal slot.

s5.title: The sidebar

plans.content: Plan document list (see the "Code workflow" topic)

s5.note: <kbd class="wph-kbd">⌘B</kbd> collapses the whole sidebar. Installed Navide plugins may add further tabs.
s5.h2: The three levels of the Agents tab
s5.p1: Top to bottom: workspace row → group row → pane row.

rows.workspace: Workspace row: left to right, the collapse arrow, a folder icon, the project name, the pane count (live / total; reclaimed panes and placeholders waiting to be restored do not count as live), the path, the fold button, ＋ and ⋯ ({more}). The context menu has, in order, {rename}, {finder}, {copyPath}, {moveToGroup} (into a workspace group; only when workspace groups exist), {reclaim}, {close} (drops the row and leaves its CLIs running for a later reopen) and {closePanes} (ends them). ↻ “{rebuildAll}” and “{history}” are not on the row; they are in the ⋯ menu: at the sidebar's narrowest width, one more button on the row would take its width from the project name, so they moved inside. ⋯ lists {rebuildAll}, {history}, {finder}, {copyPath}, {rename}, {detach} (when the workspace can be detached), {reclaim} and, when the workspace can be closed, both close actions; it flips upward near the bottom of the window, and when the menu itself is long, scrolling inside it no longer dismisses it — only scrolling elsewhere does.
rows.group: Group row: sticks to the top while scrolling and shows a status dot, the group name, the member count, a fold button that only appears on hover, and a ＋ that opens an agent inside that group. Member rows carry a neutral-colored rail along their left edge to show they belong to one group.
rows.pane: Pane row: name, status, the Docked label and so on.

callout.title: Renaming and deleting groups is not in the sidebar
callout.text: Rename / delete / detach for a group happen on its tab in the tab bar at the top; the sidebar's group row only displays it and adds panes.

s5.mode: The Agents tab's header has a two-way switch (shown only when at least one workspace exists and the window is not a detached one). {workspace} is the three-level tree described above. {free} drops the workspace and group levels and lists every agent in one flat list (child panes still indent under their parent); each row is an outlined card with a parent/workspace line under the name telling you which workspace it belongs to. In Free mode the stage shows every pane, and focusing a pane from the sidebar does not switch workspace.
s5.modeNote: The choice is stored in your user settings, so it carries over to a restart and to new windows, and windows already open follow it live; detached windows always stay in {workspace}. In Free mode, closing, rebuilding or reclaiming a tab still only acts on the current workspace's panes, and says how many panes from other workspaces were left alone. The ＋ at the far right of the header opens an agent in the current workspace in Free mode; in {workspace} mode, or with no workspace open, it opens the workspace picker.
s5.p2: Sub-panes opened by an agent or by MCP hang under their parent with 13px of indentation per level, and the parent row carries a ▾ / ▸ that collapses the whole subtree. There is no separate label — the indentation itself is what says "someone else opened this, you did not".

folds.pane: One parent pane — the ▾ / ▸ in front of the parent row; it folds that one subtree.
folds.group: A whole run group — the fold button at the right of the group row (it only appears while the pointer is on that row) collapses or expands every row in that group that has children. A group with nothing foldable has no button at all.
folds.workspace: A whole workspace — the same button on the workspace row, covering every group and subtree in that project. With nothing to fold it is disabled rather than hidden.

s5.foldNote: Alt/Option-clicking the row’s expand caret does the same thing as either fold button — the tooltip says so: Alt+click: collapse everything inside. Fold state is stored per pane, with the project, so it survives a restart.

multiselect.cmdClick: <kbd class="wph-kbd">⌘</kbd> click: add a single row to the selection.
multiselect.shiftClick: <kbd class="wph-kbd">⇧</kbd> click: select a whole range (in the order shown on screen, not the internal order).
multiselect.batchMenu: Right-clicking with several rows selected turns the menu into its batch form: Interrupt selected, Rebuild selected, Minimize selected, Restore selected, Reclaim selected (shows the eligible count), Mute selected notifications (or unmute when all selected panes are muted), and Remove selected. Reclaim keeps panes available to resume and skips protected panes.

s5.p3: Dragging any one of the selected panes takes the whole batch with it. If the row you grab is a folded parent, its hidden children come along too — only the row you actually grabbed expands into its subtree, so another folded parent in the same selection still moves alone. Where you drop decides what happens:

window.result: Hand it to another window, or detach it into a new window

s6.title: The status bar
s6.p1: The strip along the bottom of the window. It can be turned off in Settings ▸ Layout.

left.git: The Git branch name, with a * when there are uncommitted changes, followed by how far it is behind and ahead of the remote, as N↓ N↑ (each shown only when it is not zero).
left.backend: Backend pill — a status light plus the address; clickable.
left.resource: Resource pill — CPU and memory, shown only while panes are running; clickable.
left.update: Update badge — new version available / download percentage / downloaded and waiting for a restart / check failed; clickable.

s6.h2: Right half: what is in progress

right.tidying: ↻ tidying token history… N file(s) — background tidying in progress.
right.leftover: ⚠ N leftover — leftover orphan terminal processes; click to clean them up.
right.disconnected: ⚡ N conversation(s) may have been disconnected — click to recover — click to open the reconnect picker, or press ✕ to ignore it.
right.announcements: 📢 Announcement badge plus the version number and the unread count.

backend.what: The address and PID, plus Restart and Stop buttons.

announcements.what: The announcement center: release notes and notification entries, which can be expanded, marked with Mark all read, updated straight from Download / Restart to install, and extended with Load more (N left) for older ones.

clock.what: The current time, when this session started, when the project was created, and the build marker.

resource.what: CPU and memory per pane plus the total, with Reclaim N now, jump-to-pane, and opening the Resource Manager window (see the "Settings and system" topic).

callout.title: The build marker is not a clock
callout.text: The build marker in the clock popover looks like a time, but it is this version's build identifier and does not track the current time.

s7.title: Shortcut quick reference
s7.p1: The keys used in this chapter. The full list, and how to customize it, are in Settings ▸ Shortcuts.

nthCli.action: Open a pane with the Nth CLI

gitWindow.action: Open the standalone Git window (not the sidebar tab)

voice.title: Voice input
voice.p1: Hold a key and speak: Navide turns the speech into text on this machine with Whisper and types it into the input box of the CLI pane that had focus when you pressed the key. No audio leaves the computer. The feature is off by default: turn on "{enabled}" in Settings ▸ {nav}, then press Download on the "{model}" row (about 148 MB), and it is ready.

take.start: Hold the shortcut (<kbd class="wph-kbd">Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd class="wph-kbd">Alt</kbd>+<kbd class="wph-kbd">M</kbd> by default). A capsule appears at the bottom of the pane and shows the partial text it has recognised while you speak.
take.release: Release: the text goes into the input box and is not sent; read it, then press Enter yourself.
take.enter: Press <kbd class="wph-kbd">Enter</kbd> during a take to end it and send at once. If the pane could not press Enter, the capsule says the text is in the input box but was not sent.
take.esc: <kbd class="wph-kbd">Esc</kbd> cancels while recording or transcribing. While the capsule shows an error, Esc goes to the CLI instead; dismiss the error with the capsule's ✕.
take.limit: Limits: 60 seconds for a held take, 5 minutes hands-free, with a countdown over the last 10 seconds.
take.target: If the focused pane is not a CLI pane, nothing starts and the capsule says voice input only goes to CLI panes.

rows.enabled: The master switch, off by default. While it is off, the rows below are hidden.
rows.shortcut: Records a key in place. It can be a chord, a function key such as F13, a lone modifier (for example Right Option), or the fn (🌐) key on a Mac; a lone ⌘ or ⌃ starts only after being held alone for a moment, so ⌘ shortcuts keep working. Typing keys (letters, Space, Enter, Tab, Esc), chords macOS reserves and keys a Navide menu already uses are refused; a ⌘ chord is only allowed in "{toggle}" mode and must not clash with another command. A refusal says why and suggests up to three free keys. This is the same binding as the one in Settings ▸ Shortcuts; the two stay in step.
rows.fnKey: Shown only on macOS, and only while fn is the shortcut. It relies on a small listen-only helper that needs Input Monitoring permission; a failed start, a failed or timed-out permission request is reported on this row with a retry.
rows.device: Follows the system default. A chosen microphone that disappears is flagged; a silent microphone or a refused permission makes the capsule name the device.
rows.mode: Three: "{holdTap}" (the default — hold to talk and release to insert, or tap quickly to record hands-free until you press again), "{hold}" and "{toggle}".
rows.script: Whether recognised Chinese is converted; "{hantTw}" by default, or Simplified, or no conversion.
rows.model: The Whisper model. You download it once with the button; it is kept in Navide's data folder.
rows.engine: The state of the local transcription engine (including whether it uses the GPU), with a retry when it fails. It warms up when the backend connects and after the model downloads, so the first take already shows live text.

voice.note: Platforms: the fn key is macOS only; everything else works on macOS, Windows and Linux. On a few architectures (Linux arm64, Windows arm64) a package that ships without the speech engine says so on the "{engine}" row.

mcp.intro: MCP (Model Context Protocol) is a general protocol that lets an AI agent call external tools. Navide uses it in three directions that have nothing in common beyond the protocol's name — the most common source of confusion, so let's separate them first.

provide.title: Navide provides tools
provide.text: The agent in a pane can drive Navide back: read and write plans, message other panes, open new agents. Nothing to configure — it is wired up when the pane opens.

consume.title: Navide consumes docs
consume.text: The Navide backend connects to external MCP servers to read technical documentation and prepends it to a pipeline's opening prompt. Configured in Settings → MCP, and only active while a pipeline runs.

external.title: External control
external.text: Clients outside the Navide process (a script, another agent…) can drive Navide itself. Off by default; switch on "Allow external MCP clients" by hand in Settings → MCP → External access.

s1.title: Direction 1: the tools Navide gives CLI agents
s1.p1: The moment a pane starts, these appear in the agent's tool list. You do not have to teach it and there is nothing to configure — just say what you want in plain language, e.g. "mark phase two of this plan as done". There are 64 of them today (57 core, plus the 7 the Plans Navide plugin registers), alongside 3 read-only resources and 3 prompt templates.

planTools.plan_list: List every plan in this workspace, with its stage and todo progress
planTools.plan_create: Create a new plan (starting as a draft)
planTools.plan_update_stage: Advance the stage: Draft → In Review → Approved → In Progress → Done
planTools.plan_update_todo: Update the status of a single todo
planTools.plan_add_note: Record a finding or a decision
planTools.plan_add_todo: Add a todo to an existing plan

s1.note1: Plans are HTML the agent writes with these tools; you read and approve them in Navide's Plans view. The agent only starts writing code once the stage has advanced to "Approved".

workspaceTools.workspace_list: Workspaces known on this machine, including which ones have live panes; use it to get a valid path before acting on another project
workspaceTools.skills_list: Which skills the library holds, and which were delivered to this pane
workspaceTools.memory_list: The list and contents of each CLI's instruction files (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md…); read-only, and only for files on the scan list
workspaceTools.pipeline_list: Which pipelines exist, with their stage and role definitions
workspaceTools.pipeline_status: This workspace's current run state, and which stage it has reached
workspaceTools.pipeline_start: Start a pipeline run; this opens several CLI panes by stage and consumes quota
workspaceTools.pipeline_next: Advance to the next stage; refused on the last stage rather than closing the run
workspaceTools.pipeline_reset: Clear the current run's progress and tear down every pane in that window (manually opened ones included); cannot be undone
workspaceTools.pipeline_restart: Kill the existing pipeline panes and run the same task again from the top; cannot be undone
workspaceTools.pipeline_define: Create / rename / delete a pipeline, set the active one, reset the built-ins; delete and set_active are refused while a run is in progress
workspaceTools.pipeline_graph: Read or edit a pipeline as a graph: steps, approval gates, branches, joins and bounded reject loops, all in one call that applies every edit or none; refused while a run is using that pipeline
workspaceTools.pipeline_gate: Pass or reject the approval gate a running pipeline is paused on; a rejection can carry a note that is handed to the steps it sends the work back to
workspaceTools.pipeline_restart_from: Start a new run at one step instead of the first stage, reusing the earlier stages' last output; closes the pipeline's panes and opens new ones, so it spends quota
workspaceTools.stage_define: Add, edit, delete, reorder or reset stages; all four are refused while a run is using that pipeline
workspaceTools.role_define: Add, edit, rename, delete or reset roles; a rename rewrites every slot referencing it, and a role still referenced cannot be deleted
workspaceTools.scheduler_list: List Navide's scheduled jobs, including ones you may not change: each says who created it and whether you may edit it, and the answer reports the agent limits and how much of them is in use. Jobs fire only while Navide is running — nothing wakes the machine or the app
workspaceTools.scheduler_upsert: Create a scheduled job, or update one of your own by passing its id: on a timetable (every N minutes, daily or weekly at HH:MM in a time zone, or once) wake a CLI pane in your own workspace and send it an instruction. An agent's jobs are limited: 10 enabled per agent and 100 across agents, no more often than every 5 minutes, 300 runs a day between them, and a periodic job stops after 7 days unless renewed or kept by the user. A pane that names no target schedules itself
workspaceTools.scheduler_remove: Delete a scheduled job you created, together with its run history; jobs made in the Navide window, or whose creating pane has closed, are the user's
workspaceTools.scheduler_set_enabled: Pause or resume a scheduled job you created; resuming never fires a slot that passed while it was paused, and counts toward the enabled-job limits
workspaceTools.scheduler_run_now: Run a job you created once right now, outside its timetable; answers as soon as the run starts, clears a failure backoff, leaves the next scheduled slot where it was and counts toward the agents' 300 runs a day
workspaceTools.scheduler_runs: A job's run history, newest first: ok, error or skipped with its reason — a skip (no window, busy, daily cap or quota, agents' daily total, an expired agent job, a vanished target) is not an error. Any job's history can be read
workspaceTools.cli_permission_settings: Read and write the CLI permission-bypass flag (yolo). It is a global setting, not pipeline-specific, and only affects panes opened afterwards; whether a given CLI actually carries the flag is in the returned agents[].skipFlag, not the global value alone
workspaceTools.workspace_open: Open a project as a workspace in Navide; whether that is a new window or one that already has the project open is Navide's decision
workspaceTools.workspace_switch: Switch my own window to another project it already holds; panes of the project being left keep running. Refused while a pipeline is running in that window, because switching would abort it
workspaceTools.prompt_list: The prompt skills the user keeps in Settings → Prompts; read-only, since creating and editing them is the user's job
workspaceTools.mcp_list: Which MCP servers Navide connects to and which each CLI keeps in its own config, with live state and tool counts; read-only, and the same list Settings → MCP shows
workspaceTools.cli_extensions_list: Each AI CLI's own CLI extensions and hooks: type, execution tier, capabilities and who installed them. Names and metadata only; read-only, the same inventory Settings → Extensions shows
workspaceTools.credentials_list: Credentials the scan inventoried, with kind and label only; never a value
workspaceTools.credentials_findings: Credential risk findings with severity and reminder state; read-only

s1.note2: These are the things an agent cannot do with its own tools — quota, pipeline state and skill delivery are known only to Navide. Git, file access and the shell are deliberately not wrapped as MCP tools: the agent already has those abilities, a wrapper only makes them harder to use, and every pane would pay the context cost of a longer tool list.

cliTools.cli_list_targets: Which CLI panes are online, how their address is written, and whether they are busy
cliTools.cli_whoami: Who I am: pane_id, name, workspace, who opened me; pane_id is the prerequisite for acting on myself. It also names who is blocked waiting on me right now (a long waiter is about to time out, which is worth wrapping up for), and whether this machine is signed in to Navide Cloud — which decides whether panes on other machines can be addressed at all
cliTools.cli_send: Send any instruction to a named pane (same workspace, another workspace window, or another machine) and get back a msg_key to query it with; address "group" broadcasts to the other panes in my own tab group. It can be marked as a pure acknowledgement that never enters the other input box, threaded onto the message it answers, told to open a cold restore placeholder before delivering, and made to wait a while and bring the delivery outcome back
cliTools.cli_send_and_wait: Send an instruction, wait for the target to finish that turn, and bring back what it said last
cliTools.cli_check_message: Use a msg_key to see what became of a sent message: queued, delivered, or failed and why (kept for the last hour only)
cliTools.cli_open_agent: Open a new CLI pane and assign it a task; it reports back when done. A model and effort can be given, and a CLI that does not support them refuses rather than ignores them. The reply says whether the opening task actually went in — when that could not be confirmed it tells you to check the status rather than resend. Two other ways to open: reviving a cold restore placeholder in place, or naming an old CLI session id so the new pane starts with that conversation's memory
cliTools.cli_read_incoming: Read the full text of messages sent to me; by default reading consumes them so they are no longer injected into the input box, and peek reads without consuming
cliTools.cli_cancel_message: Withdraw a message that has not gone in yet; once delivery has begun it cannot be recalled, and the reply says how it ended up
cliTools.cli_read_log: Read the tail of another pane's transcript (200 lines by default), optionally with a cursor to read only what is new
cliTools.cli_get_status: Check whether another pane is busy and when it was last active, plus two more things: the identity it was launched with (which CLI, which model, which reasoning effort, whether its login has expired or it has hit a usage limit), and that CLI's quota snapshot. The quota is a cached read that is never refreshed — the returned fetch time and stale flag are exactly how old it is, and a fresh number needs the quota tool. The identity describes launch time: a model switched by typing inside the CLI is invisible here
cliTools.cli_wait_idle: Wait until another pane goes idle or the wait times out (120 seconds at most); a timeout says whether it is stuck on a permission prompt, still working, or unreachable
cliTools.cli_interrupt: Send that CLI's interrupt key to a local pane; this is not the same as stopping it — it may only clear the input box, so check the result yourself
cliTools.cli_answer_prompt: Answer a local pane's permission prompt or option menu by pressing one choice; refuses permanent allows, Guard-flagged approvals and a changed prompt, and records the answer in the pane's Guard audit
cliTools.cli_close_agent: Close another pane, the other half of cli_open_agent; this kills whatever it was doing and cannot be undone, so check with cli_get_status that it is not busy first
cliTools.cli_reclaim_agent: Reclaim a finished pane: its CLI process ends and the pane stays as a click-to-resume card, the status bar's "reclaim now". A busy, focused or not-yet-resumable pane is refused with the reason; a window older than v0.2.16 answers reclaim-unsupported
cliTools.cli_message_log: The history of messages I sent and received; once delivered a message disappears from inbox_summary and pending_incoming, and this is the only place left to find it
cliTools.cli_usage: How much quota each CLI has left; check before handing out work, or the message lands on a CLI that has already run out
cliTools.cli_failover_state: What Navide's quota failover is doing about an exhausted CLI account: the policy, open incidents, how many automatic switches the budget still allows, and any half-finished switch that blocks a vendor until the user resolves it. Read-only; accounts are named by slot, never by email
cliTools.cli_accounts_list: The CLI accounts Navide keeps and which one each CLI runs on, from the account store only: names and ids (an account Navide added on its own is named after its email), no signed-in state, since that would mean reading the credentials. Read-only
cliTools.cli_account_sign_in: Open the sign-in Navide already offers for one CLI account (a parked account in its own private home, or a claude account inside its own folder), so the user only finishes it in the browser; the user agrees first in a dialog that names the agent and its reason; nothing opens on a no or no answer. No token, code or URL comes back, nothing is switched, and the active account or a sign-in that would replace the live credential is left to the user
cliTools.cli_account_switch: Ask the user to switch one CLI to another of its accounts; the user agrees first in a dialog that names the agent, both accounts and its reason; nothing switches on a no or no answer. It goes through the window's own switch, never forced, and only the result and the accounts' display names (which can be an email) come back, never a credential
cliTools.cli_list_sessions: The CLI conversations in this workspace a new pane could be opened onto — a conversation outlives the pane that ran it: close the pane, restart the app, rebuild the pane, and the transcript stays on disk. Each row says whether it is still resumable and whether the pane that owned it is still open: do not resume a live one, which forks or corrupts it — message that pane instead
cliTools.cli_place_pane: Move a pane: change the tab group it sits in, or make it a child of another pane (the same thing as dragging it in the sidebar, through the same write path, so the position survives a restart). The two halves are independent and the reply says which landed. It does not touch that pane's CLI — nothing is sent, interrupted or restarted. Local panes only
cliTools.cli_inbox_summary: Which of the messages I sent are stale (queued for more than two minutes) or have failed. A failure notice can only be typed into the sending pane while it is idle, so an agent that works solidly for an hour receives none — this is how it goes and asks
cliTools.cli_pending_incoming: Which messages are queued for me and have not gone in yet. A message is typed into a pane only between turns, so an agent that stays busy is precisely the one that cannot be told; a non-empty answer is grounds to wrap up the turn so it can land

s1.note3: For how to use them, see the "Inter-CLI Messaging" topic. "Wait for the other side to finish" is best-effort: most CLIs (Cursor included) report the end of a turn themselves, while Kimi / Pi / Qwen are inferred from 8 seconds of silence. The returned source says how trustworthy this particular "finished" is — for those CLIs treat it as a hint, not a guarantee. If the target's window is closed or its pane killed mid-wait, source is target_lost: the message really was sent, there is simply no way left to confirm it finished — that is not a send failure, so do not resend.
s1.note4: One workspace can hold two panes with the same name, and a name alone then cannot say which one is meant, so the tools above refuse outright with ambiguous-target instead of picking one. To name a specific pane, pass the pane_id returned by cli_list_targets to cli_send, cli_send_and_wait, cli_read_log, cli_get_status or cli_wait_idle, and leave the address argument out. Names are more readable day to day; a pane reopened with a different CLI gets a new id, and on unknown-pane-id you simply look it up again. Panes on another device have no local id and can only be addressed by name.
s1.note5: Giving cli_send the address group does not look for a pane called group: it broadcasts to the other panes in my own tab group (same workspace). That differs from the bare-line protocol's all: all is the whole window, regardless of grouping. Panes in no group share one implicit group, so they can reach each other rather than nobody. The reply's shape differs too: each recipient in recipients has its own msg_key to query separately with cli_check_message, and an empty recipients means nobody else is in your group, not a failure. The cost is the same as all: a pane actually named group can no longer be addressed by name.
s1.p2: Ten of the fifteen so far: Claude Code, Codex, Copilot CLI, Qwen Code, OpenCode, Kilo Code, Kimi Code, Grok CLI, Antigravity CLI, Cursor CLI. How they are wired depends on the interface each CLI offers — a launch flag (Claude Code, Codex, Copilot, Qwen), one environment variable carrying the whole config document (OpenCode, Kilo), or a per-pane mirror of the config directory (Kimi, Grok, Antigravity). None of the three touches your own MCP config file.
s1.note6: Cursor is the one exception: it only reads .cursor/mcp.json inside the workspace, so Navide merges its entry into that file and adds it to .git/info/exclude, leaving your git status clean.
s1.note7: Not yet wired are Aider, Muse Code and Pi (those three CLIs have no MCP interface) and Droid and MiniMax Code (Navide has not wired them, and whether their CLIs expose a way in has not been established). Most of those panes can still message other panes over the bare-line output protocol; they just have no MCP tools to call. MiniMax Code is the exception: it has no output protocol either, so it can only receive.
s1.note8: The wiring happens the moment the pane starts. So after an update, panes already open still hold the old tool list — close and reopen one to get the new one.

previewTools.preview_record: Report a file I just created, modified or deleted onto this workspace's change record track; the record is stored with the workspace and survives a restart
previewTools.preview_show: Push a file, a diff or inline content straight into the user's Preview panel; it is only recorded as shown once the window owning the workspace confirms it took it
previewTools.preview_list: Read the change record track back — what other agents, the user and the file watcher each did, newest first; a timestamp cursor reads only what is new
previewTools.preview_clear: Empty the change record track; what goes is the lines the user sees in the Preview panel, the file watcher's and the user's own included, and it cannot be undone. It can also clear only what is older than a given point

s1.note9: Only four tools cross devices: send, send-and-wait, get status, and wait for idle. Reading another pane's transcript, sending an interrupt key and closing a pane all need that pane's own machine, so all three are refused. A remote pane also has no local id, making the three-part name the only handle there is; its status is the word the far window last uploaded to Navide Cloud — near-live, not live — and there is no quota snapshot either (this machine's quota cache describes this machine's logins, which is the wrong answer for a pane running elsewhere).

s2.title: Direction 2: Navide consuming external MCP
s2.p1: This is what the Settings → MCP page manages. The Navide backend connects to the MCP servers you configure, reads technical documentation relevant to the current task, and prepends it to the pipeline's opening prompt so the agent starts with the right API reference.

catalog.context7: context7 — up-to-date official docs for all sorts of frameworks and libraries
catalog.github: github — read repo, issue and PR content
catalog.filesystem: filesystem — read files in a given directory

warn.p1: Servers configured here never appear in a CLI agent's tool list. They serve one thing — "read context → inject into the opening prompt" — and fire only while a pipeline runs; panes you open by hand never touch them.
warn.p2: To let Claude Code or Codex use an MCP server itself (to query GitHub directly, say), configure it in that CLI's own MCP config, not here.

s3.title: Direction 3: external clients controlling Navide
s3.p1: The same endpoint as direction 1 (/plan-mcp) and the same set of tools; what differs is who may connect. This page opens it to clients outside the Navide process — external scripts, agents running elsewhere, any MCP client. The interface-driving tools below are often taken for external-only ones; an agent in a pane can call them too. They are listed here because an external client has no window of its own and these are all it has to drive Navide's interface with.

uiTools.ui_list_actions: List every action id currently registered in the target window
uiTools.ui_invoke: Invoke a registered action (open a new pane, switch tab, open settings…)
uiTools.ui_snapshot: Get a snapshot of the target window's current UI state (panes, tabs, focus…)
uiTools.ui_diagnostics: Read the UI action diagnostics that window recorded; use it when a tool reports success but the window behaves differently, to find out what really happened

s3.note: The action ids ui_invoke can call (ui.pane.create, ui.settings.open and so on) have to be looked up with ui_list_actions first — it lists every id the target window has registered right now, and that list is what is actually available. Called from a pane, the request goes straight to the window hosting that pane, focused or not; but if that window has since switched to another project it errors rather than running against the wrong one.

warn.p1: Anything running on this machine can control Navide while this is on. That includes opening and closing panes, messaging across workspaces, reading other panes' transcripts and driving the interface. The connection URL (which carries a one-time token) is copied from Settings → MCP → External access, and "Regenerate token" invalidates the old URL immediately.
warn.p2: The Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP) switch in the same panel is a second, lower-level escape hatch — for screenshots or for actions not yet registered, not the main route. Anything running on this machine can execute arbitrary code in Navide while this is on. Requires an app restart to take effect. Binds to 127.0.0.1 only.

s4.title: Direction 1 and direction 2 side by side

caller.provide: The CLI agent in a pane

config.provide: Nowhere — wired up when the pane opens

what.provide: Drives Navide: plans, messaging, opening agents
what.consume: Reads technical docs and attaches them to the opening prompt

noTools.symptom: The agent says it has no plan or messaging tools
noTools.detail: That pane was not wired when it opened (it predates the update), or it runs one of the five CLIs not yet wired to MCP (Aider / Droid / Muse Code / Pi / MiniMax Code). For the former, close and reopen it; for the latter, use the bare-line output protocol to message instead — MiniMax Code has not even that, and can only receive.

serverUnused.symptom: A server was added in Settings → MCP but the agent cannot use it
serverUnused.detail: That is direction 2, purely for pipelines reading docs. To let the agent call it itself, configure it in that CLI's own MCP config. The "Every CLI's MCP" section in the lower half of Settings → MCP lists, read-only, which servers each CLI has configured, so you can check directly.

planLoadFailed.symptom: The agent says the plan failed to load
planLoadFailed.detail: Every plan tool takes a workspace path. If the path the agent passes differs from the pane's actual workspace, it writes somewhere Navide cannot see. Ask it to use the pane's workspace path.

staleIdentity.symptom: It reports the pane identity as stale
staleIdentity.detail: The pane was detached to another window, or the window reloaded, and the identity recorded at wiring time expired. Reopen that pane.

externalRejected.symptom: An external client is refused (external token rejected / disabled)
externalRejected.detail: Direction 3 is off by default and "Allow external MCP clients" has to be switched on in Settings → MCP → External access first; or the token in the URL was replaced by "Regenerate token", in which case copy the latest connection URL.

unknownSession.detail: The agent tried to resume an old conversation whose id that CLI no longer has on disk. The refusal is deliberate: otherwise it would open a pane that looks like a successful resume and has actually started from nothing, which is indistinguishable without reading the transcript. Ask it to list the resumable conversations again.

staleTools.symptom: The tool list looks old (a new tool cannot be called)
staleTools.detail: Wiring happens the moment a pane starts, and an MCP tool list does not hot-reload. So after an update a pane already open still holds the old list — close and reopen that pane to get the new one.

settings.caption: Settings → MCP, the page direction 2 is managed from. Drawn in HTML rather than captured, so it follows whichever theme you are using.

nav.label: Settings sidebar
nav.text: MCP sits under Agent Assets, alongside Skills, Prompts and Memory.

actions.label: Top bar actions
actions.text: "Add MCP +" adds one from the built-in catalog, "Add custom" adds one by hand, and "Refresh" re-reads the config file.

card.label: Catalog card
card.text: One card per server, with the add button on the right; one already set up shows a grey Installed instead.

addressing.caption: Two workspace windows on the same machine. A pane name is its address; crossing workspaces only adds the folder name in front.

local.label: Same workspace
local.text: Just the pane name (reviewer, say). Without a slash it never leaves this window.

cross.label: Another workspace
cross.text: Written as folder/pane, where the folder name is the one in the other window’s title bar.

git.what: Switch to version control. A number badge in the top-right corner is the count of uncommitted changed files (over 99 shows as 99+).

plans.what: Switch to the plan document list.

plugin.name: Navide plugin-supplied
plugin.what: A tab contributed by a Navide plugin. When the Navide plugin brings no icon of its own, this diamond stands in for it.

collapse.where: Far right of the tab strip
collapse.what: Collapse the whole sidebar to a rail.
collapse.name: Collapse panel

collapseAll.what: Collapse or expand every workspace at once. When everything is collapsed, the horizontal bar in the icon gains a stroke and becomes a plus.
collapseAll.name: Collapse all folders / Expand all folders

openWorkspace.what: Bring up the workspace picker and take another project into the same window.
openWorkspace.name: Open workspace…

folderMark.name: (no tooltip)
folderMark.where: In front of every workspace name
folderMark.what: A plain marker: this row is a workspace folder.

subtree.where: Far left of the workspace row
subtree.what: Collapse the groups and panes under this workspace.
subtree.name: Expand subtree / Collapse subtree

rebuildAll.where: Right side of the workspace row
rebuildAll.what: Rebuild every resumable CLI pane in this workspace in one go. It interrupts turns in progress and reprints the conversation.

history.where: Right side of the workspace row
history.name: History

openAgent.name: Open Agent (followed by the currently selected CLI's name)
openAgent.where: Far right of the workspace row
openAgent.what: The main entry point for a new pane. It opens the Role dropdown plus the CLI list plus Terminal / Manual spawn. While the workspace path is unset it reads Set workspace path first and cannot be pressed.

newGroup.where: The flyout on the sidebar's far-left colored rail
newGroup.what: Add a workspace group (the grouping layer you only need when juggling many projects).
newGroup.name: New group

groupSubtree.where: Far left of the group row
groupSubtree.name: Expand subtree / Collapse subtree

openInGroup.where: Far right of the group row
openInGroup.what: Also opens a new pane; the difference is that it lands straight in this group.
openInGroup.name: Open an agent in this group

lineageSubtree.where: Far left of the pane row (only when it has sub-panes)
lineageSubtree.what: Collapse the whole tree of sub-panes this agent opened. Note: workspaces and groups use ›/⌄ while lineage uses ▸/▾ — two different pairs.
lineageSubtree.name: Expand subtree / Collapse subtree

autoNamed.what: A plain marker: this name was picked automatically. Rename the pane and it is gone.

stageManager.where: Beside the pane name, shown as 🎯 Mgr
stageManager.what: A plain marker: this pane is the pipeline's stage manager.

docked.where: On the pane row, shown as the icon plus Docked
docked.what: A plain label: this pane is collapsed and only its sidebar row is left.

expandRow.name: (no tooltip)
expandRow.where: Right side of the pane row
expandRow.what: Expand this row's details (session id, Interrupt and so on). Once expanded the arrow turns 90 degrees to point down.

rebuild.where: Right side of the pane row
rebuild.what: Rebuild just this one pane. With no resumable session it grays out and the tooltip changes to say to send a message first.

minimize.where: Far right of the pane row
minimize.what: Collapse the pane, leaving only this sidebar row.
minimize.name: Minimize to sidebar

managePipelines.what: Open the Roles / Pipelines manager window.

startOver.where: The Pipeline Resume card, on the button labelled ↺ Start over
startOver.what: Discard the stage progress already made and re-run from the first stage (it asks you to confirm).
startOver.name: Discard all stage progress and re-run from Stage 01

s1.title: Sidebar
s1.p1: A strip of tabs across the top of the sidebar. Expanded it shows the line icons in the table below; collapsed to a rail, Agents / Pipeline / Explorer / Plans switch to emoji (🤖 🔀 📁 📋) and only Git has no emoji — the rail keeps drawing the same SVG.

rebuild.where: Far left of the title bar
rebuild.what: Close the pane and reopen it with --resume at the current size, to clear artifacts a redraw cannot. It interrupts the turn in progress and reprints the whole conversation.

minimize.what: Collapse the pane into the sidebar and give up its slot.
minimize.name: Minimize to sidebar

autoNamed.what: A plain marker: the name was picked automatically. Double-click the title to rename and it disappears.
autoNamed.name: Named automatically from this session's first instruction — rename it and it stays yours

globalManager.where: Beside the title text, shown as 🎯 Mgr
globalManager.what: A plain marker: this is the pipeline's manager pane.

loop.what: Casts a prompt skill. Rest the pointer on it and a ring of skills fans out (5 slots at most; a longer list or a narrow pane switches to a vertical list), each slot previewing the exact text it would send. Only the skill marked default enters the ∞ loop and is re-sent at the end of every turn; every other skill sends once — no LOOP badge, no auto-continue, no turn cap.
loop.name: Loop — send the configured loop prompt to this pane

loopActive.name: ∞ Loop (the running badge)
loopActive.where: Title bar; replaces the button above once the loop is running
loopActive.what: Shows the loop's state; while waiting it counts down. Click it to deal with the current wait.

loginExpired.name: ⚠ Login expired / tooltip The CLI's login has expired — click to send its login command
loginExpired.what: This CLI's login has expired. Clicking sends the login command straight into the pane.

quotaWarn.name: The quota badge's warning state
quotaWarn.where: Far right of the title bar
quotaWarn.what: Shown when the quota cannot be read. Hover it for the reason: expired credentials, the CLI not on PATH, or a read in progress.

quota.where: Far right of the title bar
quota.what: The remaining quota. Hover it to expand the account list. While reading it shows reading; a cached value carries a Cached quota tooltip.
quota.name: Remaining quota — hover for details

activeAccount.name: (a list item, with no tooltip of its own)
activeAccount.where: The account list in the quota popover
activeAccount.what: A plain marker: the checked one is the account in use. Click another row to switch accounts.

cachedQuota.name: (no tooltip)
cachedQuota.where: In front of the percentage in the quota popover
cachedQuota.what: A plain marker: this number is an old snapshot, not a fresh read.

addAccounts.what: Jump to the CLI accounts page in Settings.
addAccounts.name: Add / manage accounts…

continue.name: ↻ Continue / tooltip This session was restored and is waiting at the prompt…
continue.what: Only appears when the pane was restored after a restart and is sitting idle at the prompt. Pressing it sends continue to pick the work back up.

resume.name: Click to resume (Resuming… while it runs)
resume.what: Bring the CLI back and carry on with the same conversation. Clicking anywhere on the card works — you do not have to aim for this button.

minimize.what: Collapse even the card into the sidebar.
minimize.name: Minimize to sidebar

s2.title: The pane itself
s2.p1: Left to right. Most buttons only appear in the matching state, so you will never see all of them at once.
s2.p2: After restarting the app, or after an idle reclaim, a pane turns into a card.

grid.where: Right end of the tab bar, 1st

sidebar.what: The focused pane takes the main area, with a column beside it listing the agents still running.

spotlight.what: The focused pane is enlarged, the rest become a thumbnail strip.

fullscreen.what: The focused pane fills the whole workspace.

auto.what: Fit every pane in automatically, with no paging.

custom.where: The two inputs at the right of the ratio row, with × between them
custom.what: Type the column and row counts yourself (1–9); press Enter or leave the field to apply.

prevPage.where: Far right of the ratio row, left of the page number
prevPage.what: The previous page of panes. Grayed out on the first page.

nextPage.what: The next page of panes. The 1/3 between them is the current page over the total.

deleteTab.what: With no panes in the tab it is deleted outright; with panes still in it, a menu first offers "Move to another group" or "Close all panes".
deleteTab.name: Delete this tab

rebuildTab.where: Very end of the tab bar
rebuildTab.what: Rebuild every resumable pane in the current tab in one go. The icon spins while it runs.

s3.title: Stage and tab bar
s3.p1: At the right end of the tab bar. All four are symbols, not image files.
s3.p2: Only appears in Grid mode with more than one pane.

branch.name: (no tooltip)
branch.where: Far left of the status bar, followed by the branch name
branch.what: Display only: the current Git branch. A * after the branch name means there are uncommitted changes.

aheadBehind.name: (no tooltip)
aheadBehind.what: Display only: how many commits behind the remote (↓) and how many ahead (↑).

backend.where: Left half of the status bar
backend.what: The backend connection state; the dot changes color with it. Click it for the address, the PID and Restart / Stop.

resources.where: Left half of the status bar, shown in the form ▤ 2 / 3 (live panes / all panes)
resources.what: How many panes are running, plus CPU and memory. Click it for per-pane usage, where you can reclaim or jump to a pane directly.
resources.name: CLI resources

updateAvailable.name: ↑ plus the version number
updateAvailable.where: Left half of the status bar
updateAvailable.what: A new version is available to download. Click to start handling the update.

updateDownloading.name: ↓ plus a percentage
updateDownloading.what: An update is downloading. When it finishes it becomes Update ready or Restart for new version; on failure, Update failed / Update check failed.

tidying.name: Backfilling historical token usage in the background, shown as ↻ tidying token history… N file(s)
tidying.where: Right half of the status bar
tidying.what: Display only: historical usage is being backfilled in the background. Nothing to do.

leftover.name: Leftover CLI processes, shown as ⚠ N leftover
leftover.where: Right half of the status bar
leftover.what: There are leftover orphan terminal processes. Click to clean them up.

disconnected.where: Right half of the status bar
disconnected.what: Panes have disconnected. Click the text to open the reconnect picker.
disconnected.name: N conversation(s) may have been disconnected — click to recover

dismiss.what: Ignore this disconnection notice and do not reconnect.
dismiss.name: Dismiss

announcements.where: Right half of the status bar, followed by the version number and the unread count
announcements.what: Open the announcement center: release notes and notifications, which can be expanded, marked all read, or used to trigger a download / install directly.
announcements.name: Announcements

time.where: Right half of the status bar
time.what: Click it for the current time, when this session started, when the project was created, and the build marker. The build marker is not a clock and does not tick.
time.name: Time

closeAll.where: Far right of the status bar
closeAll.what: Close every session and tab. History is kept.
closeAll.name: Close all sessions and tabs (history kept)

s4.title: Status bar
s4.h2: Right half: what is in progress

listView.where: Toolbar (shown while the tree view is active)
listView.what: Show changed files as a flat list.
listView.name: Switch to List View

treeView.where: Toolbar (shown while the list view is active)
treeView.what: Show changed files as a folder tree.
treeView.name: Switch to Tree View

newWindow.what: Pull the Git pane out into its own window.
newWindow.name: Open in New Window

diffReview.where: Toolbar (only while embedded in the editor window)
diffReview.what: Open a combined diff and review tab.
diffReview.name: Diff Review

moreOptions.what: The view menu: list / tree, sort by name / path / status, show ignored files. The option in effect carries a ✓ in front of it.
moreOptions.name: More options

stage.where: Changes: the file row / folder row / section header
stage.what: Stage this file, everything under this folder, or every change.

unstage.where: The matching places in Staged Changes

discard.what: Throw the edits away and restore the file to its last committed state. It asks first.

blame.what: Expand this file's history and line-by-line blame.

acceptOurs.what: Resolve the conflict by taking "our" version of the whole file.
acceptOurs.name: Accept Ours

acceptTheirs.what: Resolve the conflict by taking "their" version of the whole file.
acceptTheirs.name: Accept Theirs

folderMark.name: (no tooltip; the folder path is next to it)
folderMark.what: A plain marker. Clicking the row collapses or expands that folder.

openDiff.where: The file list under an expanded commit in History
openDiff.what: Open that file's diff for that commit in the editor.

moreOptions.what: Expand the six actions in the table below.
moreOptions.name: More options

amend.what: Fold this change into the previous commit.
amend.name: Amend Commit

commitPush.what: Commit and push to the remote straight away.

undo.what: Undo the last commit (the changes stay in the working tree).
undo.name: Undo Last Commit

generating.name: (no tooltip)
generating.what: Display only: the AI is generating a commit message for you.

branchPill.name: The branch pill (showing the current branch name)
branchPill.where: Far left of the remote action row
branchPill.what: Expand or collapse the branch panel.

account.what: Pick which Git account this workspace pushes with.
account.name: Account for this workspace

fetch.what: Fetch the remote's latest state without touching your working tree. While it runs it becomes a spinning ⟳.
fetch.name: Fetch

push.what: Push. The number after it is how many commits ahead you are; with no remote for the branch yet it becomes Publish.
push.name: Push / Publish Branch

sync.what: Pull (rebase) and push in one go.
sync.name: Sync (pull --rebase + push)

morePushOptions.where: Far right of the remote action row
morePushOptions.what: Expand Pull, Pull (rebase), Push, Push (force with lease), plus per-remote pushes when there are several.
morePushOptions.name: More pull/push options

compare.where: Every row in the branch panel (other than the current branch)
compare.what: Compare that branch with the current one.
compare.name: Compare

rebase.what: Rebase the current branch onto that one.
rebase.name: Rebase onto

merge.what: Merge that branch into the current one.
merge.name: Merge into current

showRemotes.what: Whether the list also includes remote branches.
showRemotes.name: Show remote branches / Hide remote branches

checkout.where: A remote branch row (when it does not exist locally yet)
checkout.what: Check the remote branch out as a local branch and switch to it.
checkout.name: Checkout locally

apply.where: Every row of the Stash card
apply.what: Apply this draft but keep it in the list.

pop.what: Apply it and remove the draft from the list.

openRemoteUrl.what: Open this remote's URL in the browser.
openRemoteUrl.name: Open remote URL

openInNewWindow.where: Every row of the Worktrees card
openInNewWindow.what: Open that worktree in a new window.
openInNewWindow.name: Open in New Window

lockUnlock.what: Lock or unlock this worktree so it is not pruned.
lockUnlock.name: Lock / Unlock

move.what: Move the worktree to another path.
move.name: Move

browseFolder.where: The input row for adding a worktree
browseFolder.what: Pick the location with a file picker.
browseFolder.name: Browse folder

addWorktree.where: Far right of the add-worktree row
addWorktree.what: Create the worktree from the path and branch filled in above.
addWorktree.name: Add worktree

s5.title: Git pane
s5.p1: Every button in this area is a symbol, and the same symbol repeats on folder rows, file rows and section headers — only its scope differs.

callout.title: The same symbol means different things in different areas
callout.text: ↑ is Push on the remote row and Pop on a Stash row; ⇅ is Sync on the remote row and "show remote branches" at the top of the branch panel; ✕ drops a draft in Stash and removes a worktree in Worktree. Work out which area you are in first, then look it up.

stageBadge.name: The stage badge (Draft / In Review / Approved / In Progress / Done / Abandoned)
stageBadge.what: Display only: how far this plan has got. Colors are in the table below.

todos.what: Toggle the todo list panel below.
todos.name: Todos

reviewNotes.where: Toolbar, with the unresolved count in the top-right corner
reviewNotes.what: Toggle the review notes panel. This button only appears while unresolved notes remain; with none left, the entry point moves into the ⋯ menu.

execute.name: Execute / tooltip Dispatch this approved plan to a CLI agent
execute.what: Expand the CLI agent picker and hand this plan to an agent to run. It only appears while the stage is approved.

approve.name: Approve (when disabled, the tooltip is Requires draft or in-review stage with all notes resolved)
approve.what: Set the stage to approved and stamp the approval time. It is gray while notes are unresolved or the stage is wrong.

moreActions.where: Far right of the toolbar, always present
moreActions.what: The overflow menu: Outline, Review Notes, History, Share to Git, Open in Browser, Reopen, Archive / Unarchive, Abandon, Delete, plus whichever permanent buttons have been folded in.
moreActions.name: More actions

outline.what: Expand the list of section anchors; click a heading to jump straight there.
outline.name: Outline

clearAnchor.name: Clear the section anchor
